docs.title: Tractus-X EDC
docs.text:
Java Major 0.13.0 Latest 0.12.3

The open-source, production-ready dataspace connector. Tractus-X EDC packages the Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC) with the extensions, policies and identity integration a company needs to share data in a sovereign and secure way: in Catena-X, in Manufacturing-X dataspaces such as Factory-X and Construct-X, and in any other dataspace that speaks the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) and uses the Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP) for authorization. Every part is an extension, so you can add the rules of your own dataspace.

Get started Deploy a connector Read the code Join the open meeting

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Helm (Kubernetes)Docker ComposeFull dataspace (Umbrella)Docker imagesFrom source 
helm repo add tractusx-edc https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev
helm repo update
helm search repo tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector -l   # released chart versions

helm install my-connector tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector --version <chart-version> -f my-values.yaml

No values file yet? Deploy in five minutes has copy-paste values for a local try-out, with PostgreSQL and Vault or fully in memory.

cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
# Tractus-X EDC in memory (control plane and data plane in one container): for a local try-out only,
# every restart forgets all assets, policies and contracts. The identity values are placeholders.
services:
  edc:
    image: tractusx/edc-runtime-memory:0.13.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"   # health checks: /api/check/readiness
      - "8081:8081"   # Management API
      - "8084:8084"   # Dataspace Protocol
      - "8086:8086"   # data plane public API
    environment:
      OTEL_JAVAAGENT_ENABLED: "false"
      EDC_PARTICIPANT_ID: did:web:changeme
      EDC_IAM_ISSUER_ID: did:web:changeme
      EDC_PARTICIPANT_CONTEXT_ID: try-participant-context
      TRACTUSX_EDC_PARTICIPANT_BPN: BPNL000000000001
      WEB_HTTP_PORT: "8080"
      WEB_HTTP_PATH: /api
      WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_PORT: "8081"
      WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_PATH: /management
      WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_TYPE: tokenbased
      WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_KEY: password
      WEB_HTTP_CONTROL_PORT: "8083"
      WEB_HTTP_CONTROL_PATH: /control
      WEB_HTTP_PROTOCOL_PORT: "8084"
      WEB_HTTP_PROTOCOL_PATH: /api/v1/dsp
      WEB_HTTP_PUBLIC_PORT: "8086"
      WEB_HTTP_PUBLIC_PATH: /api/public
      EDC_DSP_CALLBACK_ADDRESS: http://edc:8084/api/v1/dsp
      EDC_DATAPLANE_API_PUBLIC_BASEURL: http://localhost:8086/api/public
      TX_EDC_DATAPLANE_TOKEN_REFRESH_ENDPOINT: http://localhost:8086/api/public/token
      EDC_TRANSFER_PROXY_TOKEN_SIGNER_PRIVATEKEY_ALIAS: key-1
      EDC_TRANSFER_PROXY_TOKEN_VERIFIER_PUBLICKEY_ALIAS: key-1
      EDC_IAM_STS_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL: https://div.example.org/oauth/token
      EDC_IAM_STS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: try-client-id
      EDC_IAM_STS_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET_ALIAS: try-client-secret
      TX_EDC_IAM_STS_DIV_URL: https://div.example.org
      TX_EDC_IAM_DCP_BDRS_SERVER_URL: https://bdrs.example.org
EOF

docker compose up -d
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8081/management/v3/assets/request \
  -H "X-Api-Key: password" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"@context": {"@vocab": "https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/"}, "@type": "QuerySpec"}'

The same settings the tractusx-connector-memory chart sets; see Configuration for the rest. To exchange data with a partner, the connector needs a real wallet: see the next tab. For a generated Compose setup with a provider and a consumer, try the Tractus-X Starter Kit.

git clone https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractus-x-umbrella.git
cd tractus-x-umbrella/charts/umbrella
helm dependency update
helm install -f values-adopter-decentralized-identityhub.yaml umbrella . --namespace umbrella --create-namespace

The Tractus-X Umbrella runs a whole dataspace on your own cluster: a provider and a consumer Tractus-X EDC, each with its own Tractus-X Identity Hub as wallet, an IssuerService and the BDRS. Start with its guide for this setup (cluster prerequisites for Linux, macOS and Windows are linked there).

docker pull tractusx/edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault:<version>
docker pull tractusx/edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault:<version>
docker pull tractusx/edc-runtime-memory:<version>     # testing only

Multi-architecture (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), non-root, published on Docker Hub for every release. Settings come from environment variables; see Configuration.

git clone https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc.git
cd tractusx-edc
./gradlew build          # compile, unit tests, Checkstyle (JDK 21)
./gradlew dockerize      # local images of every runtime

Then follow Developer setup or the local quick start.

docs.title: Why Tractus-X EDC?
docs.text:
Upstream EDC is a framework you assemble a connector from. Tractus-X EDC is that connector, ready to run in Catena-X, Manufacturing-X and other dataspaces:

  • Released runtimes and OSS images on Docker Hub, for every release
  • Helm charts with PostgreSQL and Vault options, tested on every CI run
  • Catena-X policies, BPN groups and BDRS built in, and room for your own
  • Extensible: add the policies and services of your dataspace as extensions
  • Any DCP wallet: Tractus-X Identity Hub, SAP DIV or your own
  • A mature release cycle: quarterly releases with release candidates and backported fixes, aligned with Eclipse Tractus-X
  • An open roadmap: companies join the public planning and contribute to it
  • Migrations and upgrade guides for every release, upgradeability tested in CI
  • Security scans and Eclipse license checks of every dependency
  • An open community with a public Connector Open Meeting
  • Production-ready and running in Catena-X today

Why Tractus-X EDC Who uses it

Use in production, at your own risk

Tractus-X EDC is built, tested and released for production use, and runs in production in Catena-X. Like any open-source software it comes without warranty (Apache License 2.0, sections 7 and 8): you operate it, and you are responsible for securing, configuring and updating it. Start with the production checklist.

Tractus-X EDC is its reference implementation: production-ready, in use throughout the Catena-X dataspace, and reused by other dataspaces such as Construct-X.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text: This section explains how a Tractus-X EDC connector is built and how it talks to the rest of the dataspace. Read it top to bottom once; afterwards each page works as a reference.

docs.title: System context
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  subgraph you[Your company]
    apps[Your applications<br/>and backends]
    subgraph connector[Tractus-X EDC connector]
      cp[Control plane]
      dp[Data plane]
    end
    vault[(Vault)]
    db[(PostgreSQL)]
  end
  subgraph partner[Partner company]
    pcp[Partner control plane]
    pdp[Partner data plane]
  end
  subgraph ds[Dataspace services]
    wallet[Credential service<br/>and STS]
    bdrs[BDRS<br/>BPN ↔ DID]
    issuer[Credential issuer]
  end

  apps -- "Management API" --> cp
  cp <-- "Dataspace Protocol (DSP)" --> pcp
  dp <-- "data (HTTP, S3, Azure Blob, …)" --> pdp
  cp -- "signaling" --> dp
  cp -- "DCP: tokens and presentations" --> wallet
  cp -- "resolve BPN / DID" --> bdrs
  issuer -. "issues credentials" .-> wallet
  cp --> db
  dp --> db
  cp --> vault
  dp --> vault

Three conversations happen at the same time:

  1. Your applications ↔ your control plane over the Management API: you describe what you offer, or what you want to consume.
  2. Your control plane ↔ the partner's control plane over the Dataspace Protocol (DSP): catalog, contract negotiation and transfer process. Every DSP request carries a token, and the receiver checks the sender's verifiable credentials via the Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP).
  3. Data plane ↔ data plane (or partner application ↔ your data plane): the actual data, protected by a short-lived token from the transfer.

docs.title: How Tractus-X EDC relates to upstream EDC
docs.text:
Tractus-X EDC is not a fork. It is a set of extensions and runtime distributions on top of the upstream Eclipse Dataspace Components:

flowchart LR
  up["Upstream EDC<br/>(BOMs: control plane, data plane,<br/>DCP, SQL features)"] --> base["Tractus-X base runtimes<br/>edc-controlplane-base<br/>edc-dataplane-base"]
  tx["Tractus-X extensions<br/>policies, BDRS, EDR API,<br/>token refresh, DSP 0.8, …"] --> base
  base --> dist["Distributions<br/>PostgreSQL + Vault<br/>in-memory"]
  dist --> img["Docker images<br/>and Helm charts"]

The upstream version this release builds on is pinned in gradle/libs.versions.toml (the edc entry). See Code architecture for the module layout.

docs.title: Protocols at a glance
docs.text:
Protocol Between Versions in Tractus-X EDC Dataspace Protocol (DSP) Control plane ↔ control plane 2025-1 (default, path /2025-1) and the legacy v0.8 (path /, kept for downward compatibility) Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP) Connector ↔ credential service v1.0 Data plane signaling Control plane ↔ data plane upstream EDC signaling API (/v1/dataflows) Management API Your apps ↔ control plane v3 (plus Tractus-X endpoints)

The consumer chooses the DSP version with the protocol field in Management API requests: dataspace-protocol-http:2025-1 or the legacy dataspace-protocol-http. The connector discovery endpoint tells you which version a partner supports.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A Tractus-X EDC connector consists of a control plane and one or more data planes, plus external services for state, secrets and identity.

flowchart LR
  subgraph CP[Control plane]
    direction TB
    mgmt[Management API<br/>:8081 /management]
    dsp["Protocol API (DSP)<br/>:8084 /api/v1/dsp"]
    ctrl[Control API<br/>:8083 /control]
    core[Catalog · Negotiation · Transfer<br/>Policy engine · EDR cache]
    mgmt --> core
    dsp --> core
    ctrl --> core
  end
  subgraph DP[Data plane]
    direction TB
    pub[Public API<br/>:8081 /api/public]
    dpctrl[Control API<br/>:8084 /api/control]
    proxy[Consumer proxy<br/>:8186 /proxy]
    pipe[Pipelines and token service]
    pub --> pipe
    dpctrl --> pipe
    proxy --> pipe
  end
  core -- "start / suspend / terminate<br/>/v1/dataflows" --> dpctrl
  pipe -- "registration /v1/dataplanes<br/>status: complete / fail" --> ctrl

Ports and paths are the Helm chart defaults.

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text:
The control plane is the "brain". It never touches the data itself.

It is responsible for:

  • Catalog. Builds the catalog a requesting partner may see, by evaluating the access policy of every contract definition.
  • Contract negotiation. Runs the negotiation state machine as consumer or provider and stores agreements.
  • Transfer process. Starts, suspends and terminates transfers; asks a data plane to do the work.
  • Policy engine. Evaluates ODRL policies with the constraint functions of the dataspace, in Catena-X those of cx-policy. See Catena-X policies.
  • Identity. Obtains tokens from the STS, requests and verifies verifiable presentations, resolves BPNs and DIDs via BDRS in Catena-X. See Identity and trust.
  • EDR cache. Stores the endpoint data references (EDRs) it receives as a consumer and refreshes their tokens. See EDRs and token refresh.

Its APIs:

API Audience Exposure Management API Your own applications Internal only; protected by an API key or delegated (JWT) auth Protocol API (DSP) Partner connectors Public, via TLS ingress Control API Your data planes Internal only Default API (/api/check/*) Kubernetes probes Internal only

docs.title: Data plane
docs.text:
The data plane is the "muscle". It moves data, or proxies requests to your backend.

It is responsible for:

  • Provider pull (HTTP). Its public API accepts requests from consumers that present a valid access token and proxies them to the asset's backend.
  • Provider push. Pushes data to a destination given by the consumer (HTTP, AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage).
  • Tokens. Issues the access token and refresh token of each EDR and serves the refresh endpoint (POST /token on the public API).
  • Consumer proxy. A convenience API (POST /proxy/aas/request) that lets your applications fetch provider data using the EDRs cached in your own control plane.
  • Non-finite push. Keeps push flows open and re-pushes on demand (POST /v3/dataflows/{id}/trigger on the data plane's management context).

How it connects to the control plane:

  1. At startup the data plane registers itself at the control plane's selector (/v1/dataplanes), announcing the source and transfer types it supports.
  2. When a transfer starts, the control plane calls the data plane's signaling API (/v1/dataflows).
  3. When a push transfer ends, the data plane reports complete or fail back to the control plane.

docs.text:
Runtime Contains Stores Vault edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault Control plane PostgreSQL HashiCorp Vault edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault Data plane PostgreSQL HashiCorp Vault edc-runtime-memory Control plane and data plane in one JVM In memory In memory, single participant

docs.text: Dependency Used by For PostgreSQL Control plane, data plane All state: assets, policies, negotiations, transfers, EDRs, tokens HashiCorp Vault Control plane, data plane Secrets: STS client secret, token signing keys, credentials of data addresses Credential service (wallet) and STS Control plane, data plane Self-issued tokens and verifiable presentations (DCP) BDRS Control plane Mapping BPNs to DIDs and back (Catena-X) OpenTelemetry collector (optional) Both Traces, metrics and business events

docs.title: What Tractus-X adds
docs.text:
Compared to a plain upstream EDC, the Tractus-X runtimes add, among others:

  • the Catena-X policy functions (cx-policy) and policy validation at creation time;
  • business partner groups and the /v3/business-partner-groups API;
  • the BDRS client for BPN ↔ DID resolution;
  • the EDR API /v3/edrs (negotiate and transfer in one call, cached and refreshed tokens);
  • token refresh on the provider data plane and in the consumer;
  • the DSP 0.8 backport for downward compatibility;
  • connector discovery /v3/connectordiscovery;
  • agreement retirement /v3/contractagreements/retirements;
  • the DIV STS client and DID document service self-registration.

The extension catalogue lists every module.

docs.title: EDRs and token refresh
docs.text: An Endpoint Data Reference (EDR) is what a consumer receives when a pull transfer starts: the address of the provider's data plane and a short-lived access token to call it. Tractus-X EDC caches EDRs for you and keeps their tokens fresh, so your applications can keep using a transfer for as long as the agreement allows.

docs.title: What an EDR looks like
docs.text:
{
  "@type": "DataAddress",
  "type": "https://w3id.org/idsa/v4.1/HTTP",
  "endpoint": "https://provider-data.plane/api/public",
  "authorization": "eyJ…",
  "tx-auth:refreshEndpoint": "https://provider-data.plane/api/public/token",
  "tx-auth:refreshToken": "eyJ…",
  "tx-auth:expiresIn": "300",
  "tx-auth:refreshAudience": "did:web:provider.example.com"
}
Field Meaning endpoint Base URL of the provider data plane's public API authorization Access token. Send it as the Authorization header tx-auth:expiresIn Token lifetime in seconds (provider default 300) tx-auth:refreshEndpoint Where to exchange the refresh token for a new token pair tx-auth:refreshToken One-time refresh token tx-auth:refreshAudience Audience for the self-issued token that authenticates the refresh request

The tx-auth prefix stands for https://w3id.org/tractusx/auth/. The EDR, including its tokens, is stored in the consumer's Vault; the cache index lives in the database.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Cached: TransferProcessStarted<br/>(EDR received)
  Cached --> Cached: GET …/dataaddress?auto_refresh=true<br/>(refresh if expired or close to expiry)
  Cached --> Cached: POST …/refresh<br/>(forced refresh)
  Cached --> [*]: transfer SUSPENDED or TERMINATED<br/>or DELETE /v3/edrs/{id}

The EDR follows its transfer process: as long as the transfer is STARTED, the EDR is in the cache. When the transfer is suspended or terminated, the EDR is removed automatically.

docs.title: Getting a valid token
docs.text:
Call Behaviour GET /v3/edrs/{transferProcessId}/dataaddress Returns the EDR. With auto_refresh=true (the default) the token is refreshed first if it has expired or is about to. With auto_refresh=false it is returned as is. POST /v3/edrs/{transferProcessId}/refresh Forces a refresh and returns the new EDR. POST /proxy/aas/request on the consumer data plane Looks up the EDR (by assetId + providerId, or transferProcessId), refreshes it if needed and fetches the data for you.

Concurrent refreshes of the same EDR are serialised with a database row lock, so several application instances can share one connector safely.

docs.title: How a refresh works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant STS as Consumer STS
  participant PDP as Provider data plane
  CCP->>STS: self-issued token, audience = tx-auth:refreshAudience
  STS-->>CCP: ID token
  CCP->>PDP: POST {refreshEndpoint}<br/>grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=…<br/>Authorization: Bearer <ID token>
  PDP->>PDP: validate refresh token and caller identity
  PDP-->>CCP: new access token, new refresh token, expires_in
  CCP->>CCP: update EDR in the cache

The refresh token is rotated on each refresh. The previous token stays valid until the new one is used for the first time, so a lost response does not break the flow (see ADR: refresh token retire on acknowledgement).

docs.title: Provider-side settings
docs.text: Helm value Setting Default (chart) Meaning dataplane.token.refresh.expiry_seconds tx.edc.dataplane.token.expiry 300 Access token lifetime dataplane.token.refresh.expiry_tolerance_seconds tx.edc.dataplane.token.expiry.tolerance 10 Clock skew tolerance dataplane.token.refresh.refresh_endpoint tx.edc.dataplane.token.refresh.endpoint <public URL>/token Refresh endpoint put into EDRs dataplane.token.signer.privatekey_alias edc.transfer.proxy.token.signer.privatekey.alias – Vault alias of the signing key dataplane.token.verifier.publickey_alias edc.transfer.proxy.token.verifier.publickey.alias – Vault alias of the verification key

docs.title: Data exchange flows
docs.text:
This page shows, as sequence diagrams, what happens between the control planes and data planes of consumer and provider. Identity checks (see Identity and trust) happen on every DSP call and are drawn only once.

flowchart LR
  d[Discovery<br/>optional] --> c[Catalog] --> n[Negotiation] --> t[Transfer] --> data[Data access]

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant PCP as Provider control plane
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/catalog/request (counterPartyAddress, counterPartyId, protocol)
  CCP->>CCP: compute credential scopes, get token from STS
  CCP->>PCP: DSP CatalogRequestMessage + token
  PCP->>PCP: verify identity (DCP), then for each contract definition evaluate its ACCESS policy
  PCP-->>CCP: DCAT catalog: datasets with offers (odrl:hasPolicy) and distributions
  CCP-->>App: catalog

The offers contain the contract policy. Distributions tell you the transfer types the provider supports, such as HttpData-PULL, HttpData-PUSH, AmazonS3-PUSH or AzureStorage-PUSH.

docs.title: Contract negotiation
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant PCP as Provider control plane
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/contractnegotiations (offer policy, counterPartyAddress, protocol)
  CCP-->>App: 200 { @id: negotiationId }
  CCP->>PCP: DSP ContractRequestMessage
  PCP->>PCP: check offer matches contract definition, evaluate CONTRACT policy
  PCP->>CCP: ContractAgreementMessage
  CCP->>PCP: ContractAgreementVerificationMessage
  PCP->>CCP: ContractNegotiationEventMessage (FINALIZED)
  App->>CCP: GET /v3/contractnegotiations/{id}
  CCP-->>App: state FINALIZED, contractAgreementId

The negotiation is asynchronous: poll its state, or register a callback. Both sides store the agreement, and Tractus-X EDC also records the BPNs of both parties with it.

docs.title: Transfer: consumer pull (HTTP)
docs.text:
The most common pattern in Catena-X. The provider data plane becomes a protected proxy in front of the provider's backend, and the consumer receives an EDR (endpoint + token).

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant PCP as Provider control plane
  participant PDP as Provider data plane
  participant BE as Provider backend
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/transferprocesses (contractId, transferType HttpData-PULL)
  CCP->>PCP: DSP TransferRequestMessage
  PCP->>PCP: evaluate agreement policy (transfer scope), check agreement not retired
  PCP->>PDP: start data flow (/v1/dataflows)
  PDP-->>PCP: EDR: endpoint, access token, refresh token, refresh endpoint
  PCP->>CCP: TransferStartMessage with EDR
  CCP->>CCP: store EDR in cache
  App->>CCP: GET /v3/edrs/{transferProcessId}/dataaddress
  CCP-->>App: endpoint + token (refreshed if needed)
  App->>PDP: GET {endpoint}/{path} with Authorization: {token}
  PDP->>PDP: validate token
  PDP->>BE: proxied request
  BE-->>PDP: data
  PDP-->>App: data

The transfer stays in state STARTED until it is terminated or suspended, or until the policy monitor ends it (for example when DataUsageEndDate is reached). Tokens are short-lived and refreshed; see EDRs and token refresh.

docs.title: Transfer: provider push
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant PCP as Provider control plane
  participant PDP as Provider data plane
  participant Dest as Consumer destination
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/transferprocesses (transferType e.g. HttpData-PUSH, dataDestination)
  CCP->>PCP: DSP TransferRequestMessage
  PCP->>PDP: start data flow
  PDP->>Dest: push data (HTTP, S3, Azure Blob)
  PDP->>PCP: complete
  PCP->>CCP: TransferCompletionMessage

Non-finite push. If the asset's data address has "isNonFinite": "true", the flow stays open after the first push. The provider re-pushes the full current content with POST /v3/dataflows/{transferProcessId}/trigger on the data plane management API. See the walkthrough.

docs.title: One call: negotiate and transfer with the EDR API
docs.text:
POST /v3/edrs starts a negotiation; when it is finalized, the connector automatically starts an HttpData-PULL transfer and caches the resulting EDR.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant PCP as Provider control plane
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/edrs (offer, counterPartyAddress, protocol)
  CCP->>PCP: negotiation …
  PCP-->>CCP: agreement (FINALIZED)
  CCP->>PCP: transfer request HttpData-PULL (automatic)
  PCP-->>CCP: TransferStartMessage with EDR
  CCP->>CCP: cache EDR
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/edrs/request (filter by assetId, agreementId, …)
  CCP-->>App: EDR entries (transferProcessId)
  App->>CCP: GET /v3/edrs/{transferProcessId}/dataaddress

docs.title: Connector discovery
docs.text:
Before the first catalog request you need the partner's DSP address and protocol version.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant App as Consumer app
  participant CCP as Consumer control plane
  participant DID as Partner DID document
  participant PCP as Partner control plane
  App->>CCP: POST /v3/connectordiscovery/connectors (counterPartyId = partner DID)
  CCP->>DID: resolve DID, read services of type DataService
  loop each connector
    CCP->>PCP: GET /.well-known/dspace-version
    PCP-->>CCP: supported DSP versions
  end
  CCP-->>App: [{ protocol, counterPartyId, counterPartyAddress }, …]

For a single known address, POST /v3/connectordiscovery/dspversionparams returns the parameters to use directly. A partner that only speaks DSP 0.8 is detected too, and you get its BPNL as counterPartyId.

docs.title: Agreement retirement
docs.text: A provider can retire an agreement before its natural end with POST /v3/contractagreements/retirements. New transfers for it are rejected and the policy monitor terminates running ones. DELETE /v3/contractagreements/retirements/{agreementId} reactivates it. See the agreements README.

docs.title: Identity and trust
docs.text: A connector must answer two questions on every request it receives: who is calling, and what is the caller allowed to do. Tractus-X EDC answers both with decentralized identity: DIDs, verifiable credentials and the Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP).

docs.title: The actors
docs.text: Actor What it is In Tractus-X EDC DID The connector's identifier, e.g. did:web:connector.example.com. Resolves to a DID document with keys and service endpoints. participant.id (setting edc.participant.id) BPNL The business partner number of the company, as used in Catena-X. participant.bpnl (setting tractusx.edc.participant.bpn) Credential service (wallet) Holds the company's verifiable credentials and creates verifiable presentations (VPs). External. Found through the DID document. STS Secure Token Service. Issues self-issued ID tokens the connector attaches to its DSP requests. External; reached via OAuth2 client credentials (dcp.sts.oauth.*). A DIV flavour is used when dcp.sts.div.url is set. Trusted issuers The DIDs whose credentials you accept. dcp.trustedIssuers BDRS BPN-DID Resolution Service: a directory mapping BPNLs to DIDs. controlplane.bdrs.server.url

docs.title: Wallets you can use
docs.text:
Tractus-X EDC talks to the wallet only through DCP and an STS, so any DCP-compliant wallet works. In use today:

Wallet What it is Connector settings Tractus-X Identity Hub Open-source DCP wallet and IssuerService of Eclipse Tractus-X, built on the upstream EDC Identity Hub. You run it yourself, next to the connector. dcp.sts.oauth.* pointing to the Identity Hub STS SAP Decentralized Identity Verification (DIV) Managed wallet operated by SAP, used by many Catena-X participants. dcp.sts.oauth.* and dcp.sts.div.url Your own Any wallet that implements the credential service and STS of DCP. dcp.sts.oauth.*

To see a connector working with the Identity Hub end to end, deploy the Tractus-X Umbrella with its Identity Hub setup.

docs.title: The Catena-X credentials
docs.text:
Catena-X defines the credentials below and Tractus-X EDC requests them out of the box. Other dataspaces, for example in Manufacturing-X, define their own credential types: the connector asks for whatever credentials the policies being evaluated reference, and further rules can be added as extensions.

Credential Says that… Requested when MembershipCredential the company is a Catena-X member Always (default scope) DataExchangeGovernanceCredential the company signed the data exchange governance framework agreement Default scope for DSP 2025-1; checked by the FrameworkAgreement constraint BpnCredential the DID belongs to this BPNL Default scope for DSP 2025-1 Others (e.g. DismantlerCredential) special roles When a policy references them

The connector derives the scopes it asks for from two sources: default scopes per DSP version, and the left operands of the policies being evaluated (for example FrameworkAgreement → DataExchangeGovernanceCredential). Scopes have the form org.eclipse.tractusx.vc.type:<CredentialType>:read.

docs.title: How a DSP request is authenticated
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant C as Consumer control plane
  participant STS as Consumer STS
  participant P as Provider control plane
  participant CS as Consumer credential service
  C->>STS: request self-issued token (audience = provider DID, scopes)
  STS-->>C: ID token (contains an access token for the credential service)
  C->>P: DSP request + Authorization: Bearer <ID token>
  P->>P: resolve consumer DID document, verify token signature
  P->>CS: presentation query (scopes) with the embedded access token
  CS-->>P: verifiable presentation
  P->>P: verify VP signatures, issuers (trusted?), revocation, expiry
  P->>P: evaluate policy with the verified claims
  P-->>C: DSP response

Verifiable presentation cache. To avoid querying the credential service on every request, the provider caches VPs. Configure with dcp.cache.enabled (default true) and dcp.cache.validity (seconds, default 86400).

docs.title: BPN ↔ DID resolution with BDRS
docs.text:
Catena-X policies and many applications speak in BPNLs, while DSP 2025-1 identifies participants by DID. The BDRS client bridges the two:

  • It downloads the BPN directory from {bdrs}/bpn-directory, authenticated with the connector's own Membership VP, and caches it (controlplane.bdrs.cache_validity_seconds, chart default 600).
  • When you address a partner by BPNL, the connector maps it to the DID audience of the outgoing token.
  • When a policy checks BPNs (for example BusinessPartnerGroup), the connector maps the caller's DID to its BPNL.

docs.title: Participant identity per protocol version
docs.text:
DSP version Protocol id Participant identity 2025-1 dataspace-protocol-http:2025-1 DID 0.8 (legacy) dataspace-protocol-http BPNL, taken from the holderIdentifier of the Membership credential

The legacy DSP 0.8 sends the Authorization header without a Bearer prefix. The token-interceptor extension adds or strips the prefix so that both versions work side by side.

docs.title: Publishing your connector in your DID document
docs.text: Partners discover your connector through the DataService entry in your DID document. With dcp.didService.selfRegistration.enabled: true, the control plane adds this entry at startup (pointing to your DSP /.well-known/dspace-version endpoint) and, for single-replica deployments, removes it at shutdown. The entry id is derived from the participant context id. The DIV implementation updates the DID document through the DIV wallet API.

docs.title: Settings at a glance
docs.text: Helm value Setting participant.id edc.participant.id, edc.iam.issuer.id participant.bpnl tractusx.edc.participant.bpn dcp.sts.oauth.token_url / .client.id / .client.secret_alias edc.iam.sts.oauth.token.url / .client.id / .client.secret.alias dcp.sts.div.url tx.edc.iam.sts.div.url dcp.trustedIssuers edc.iam.trusted-issuer.<n>-issuer.id, ….supportedtypes dcp.cache.enabled / dcp.cache.validity tx.edc.dcp.cache.enabled / tx.edc.dcp.cache.validity.seconds controlplane.bdrs.server.url tx.edc.iam.dcp.bdrs.server.url dcp.didService.selfRegistration.enabled tx.edc.did.service.self.registration.enabled

docs.text:
• DCP specification
  • BDRS client README
  • DCP extensions README
  • ADR: verifiable presentation caching
  • ADR: DID service registration

docs.title: Persistence and state
docs.text: A connector keeps two kinds of state: records (assets, policies, negotiations, transfers, EDR index, …) in PostgreSQL, and secrets (keys, tokens, credentials of data addresses) in HashiCorp Vault.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Both production runtimes use PostgreSQL. In the official chart, control plane and data plane share one database and schema.

Owner Tables Control plane (upstream) edc_asset, edc_policydefinitions, edc_contract_definitions, edc_contract_negotiation, edc_contract_agreement, edc_transfer_process, edc_policy_monitor, edc_data_plane_instance, edc_edr_entry, edc_lease, edc_jti_validation Control plane (Tractus-X) edc_business_partner_group, edc_agreement_retirement, edc_contract_agreement_bpns Data plane edc_data_plane, edc_accesstokendata

Connection settings:

Setting Meaning edc.datasource.default.url, .user, .password Default data source used by all stores edc.sql.store.<store>.datasource Optional: a different named data source for one store

docs.title: Schema migrations with Flyway
docs.text:
The schema is created and upgraded automatically at startup by the connector-migration extension, which is part of both production runtimes.

flowchart LR
  start[Runtime starts] --> check{tx.edc.postgresql.migration.enabled?}
  check -- "true (default)" --> fw[Flyway migrate<br/>classpath:migrations/connector<br/>history: flyway_schema_history]
  check -- false --> run
  fw --> run[Extensions start]
Setting Default Meaning tx.edc.postgresql.migration.enabled true Run migrations at startup tx.edc.postgresql.migration.schema public Target schema

Things to know:

  • The migrations live in edc-extensions/migrations/connector-migration/src/main/resources/migrations/connector/. Existing databases are baselined at version 1.0.0.
  • The runtime refuses to start without edc.participant.context.id, because it is used as a value in the migrated data. Never change it after the first start.
  • Run one migration at a time: when you roll out a new version, let one pod finish its startup before scaling up.
  • If you want to run migrations from a pipeline instead, disable them in the runtime and apply the same scripts with Flyway yourself.

Adding or reviewing a migration is described in the sql-migration skill of the Connector Sensei.

docs.title: Vault
docs.text:
Secrets are never stored in the database. The connector reads and writes them in Vault by alias:

Secret Referenced by STS / DIV OAuth client secret dcp.sts.oauth.client.secret_alias Private key for signing data plane tokens dataplane.token.signer.privatekey_alias Public key for verifying data plane tokens dataplane.token.verifier.publickey_alias Cached EDRs (tokens) Written by the consumer control plane Credentials of an asset's backend dataAddress properties that name a secret alias

The HashiCorp Vault client uses the KV engine at vault.hashicorp.paths.secret (default /v1/secret), with an optional folder prefix for all keys.

docs.title: The in-memory runtime
docs.text: edc-runtime-memory has no database and no Vault: all records and secrets live in the JVM and are lost on restart. Secrets can be seeded at startup with tx.edc.vault.secrets (key1:secret1;key2:secret2). Use it only for development and tests.

docs.title: Catena-X policies
docs.text: Policies decide who sees an offer and under which conditions data may be used. EDC policies are ODRL written in JSON-LD. Tractus-X EDC adds the Catena-X constraints defined in the standard CX-0152 Policy Constraints for Data Exchange. These constraints are specific to Catena-X; other dataspaces add their own policy rules as extensions.

docs.title: Access policy vs contract policy
docs.text:
A contract definition links assets to two policies:

flowchart LR
  cd[Contract definition] -- accessPolicyId --> ap["Access policy<br/>action: access"]
  cd -- contractPolicyId --> up["Contract (usage) policy<br/>action: use"]
  cd -- assetsSelector --> assets[Assets]
  ap -. "evaluated at" .-> cat[Catalog request]
  up -. "evaluated at" .-> neg[Negotiation]
  up -. "becomes part of" .-> agr[Agreement]
  agr -. "evaluated at" .-> tp[Transfer start<br/>and policy monitor]
Access policy Contract (usage) policy Action access (cx-policy:access) use (odrl:use) Question it answers "May this partner see the offer?" "On which terms may this partner use the data?" Evaluated On every catalog request During negotiation; the agreement's policy again at transfer time Typical constraints Membership, FrameworkAgreement, BusinessPartnerGroup FrameworkAgreement and UsagePurpose (both mandatory), plus use-case terms

The contract-definition-policies validator enforces the split: a contract definition's accessPolicyId must reference a policy with action access, and its contractPolicyId one with action use.

Every Catena-X usage policy needs two constraints

A usage policy must contain at least FrameworkAgreement (e.g. DataExchangeGovernance:1.0) and UsagePurpose, combined with and. Offers without them are not accepted in the Catena-X dataspace.

docs.title: An example pair
Validation at creation time
docs.text:
With controlplane.policy.validation.enabled: true (the default), POST /v3/policydefinitions rejects policies with unknown constraints, wrong operators or forbidden combinations. Each constraint has a JSON schema in edc-extensions/cx-policy/src/main/resources/jsonschema/cx-policy/. For example:

  • BusinessPartnerGroup and BusinessPartnerNumber accept isAnyOf / isNoneOf with an array of values.
  • UsagePurpose accepts isAnyOf with an array of known purposes.
  • Membership must be eq "active".

Keep validation on

The policy engine treats a constraint it has no function for as satisfied. A typo in a left operand can therefore silently open an offer to everyone. Validation catches this before the policy is stored.

docs.title: Which constraint goes where
docs.text:
Constraint Action Rule type Membership, FrameworkAgreement access, use permission (checked against the partner's verifiable credentials) BusinessPartnerGroup, BusinessPartnerNumber access permission (checked against the partner's BPN) UsagePurpose, ContractReference, ContractTermination, ConfidentialInformationMeasures, ConfidentialInformationSharing, DataFrequency, DataUsageEndDate, DataUsageEndDefinition, DataUsageEndDurationDays, ExclusiveUsage, JurisdictionLocation, JurisdictionLocationReference, Liability, Precedence, VersionChanges, Warranty, WarrantyDefinition, WarrantyDurationMonths use permission AffiliatesBpnl, AffiliatesRegion use permission or prohibition UsageRestriction use prohibition DataProvisioningEndDate, DataProvisioningEndDurationDays use obligation

Many use-case terms (for example Warranty) are contractual: the connector checks that they are well-formed and records them in the agreement, but it cannot enforce them technically. The source of truth is PolicyValidationConstants; the policy walkthrough explains each constraint.

docs.title: Business partner groups
docs.text:
Instead of listing BPNs in every policy, keep groups in the connector and reference them:

{ "leftOperand": "BusinessPartnerGroup", "operator": "isAnyOf", "rightOperand": ["gold-customers"] }

You manage the BPN → group assignment with the /v3/business-partner-groups API. Groups can change at any time without touching the policy. At catalog time the connector resolves the caller's BPN and looks up its groups. In the 2025-09 namespace, BusinessPartnerGroup and BusinessPartnerNumber are evaluated only in the catalog scope. See Tutorial 2.

docs.title: Legacy namespace
docs.text: Policies written with the old namespace https://w3id.org/catenax/policy/ are still evaluated by the cx-policy-legacy extension, so existing agreements keep working. New policies should use the 2025-09 context.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Policy walkthrough
  • BPN validation README
  • Catena-X standards

docs.title: Supported dataspaces
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC started as the connector of the Catena-X automotive dataspace. Since then, more dataspaces have emerged, many of them under the Manufacturing-X umbrella, and they need the same connector without the Catena-X specific parts. The multi-dataspace support ADR (January 2026) therefore turns Tractus-X EDC into a dataspace-agnostic core with dataspace-specific flavours, and makes it the one place where all of them are developed.

docs.title: Status per dataspace
docs.text:
Dataspace Connector Status Catena-X (automotive) Tractus-X EDC, this repository Supported and released. Every Tractus-X release, images on Docker Hub, Helm charts. In production. Factory-X (manufacturing, Manufacturing-X) Factory-X EDC Developed externally on Tractus-X EDC as midstream, today by excluding the Catena-X modules. Proof of concept; may be merged here when it reaches production status. Construct-X (construction, Manufacturing-X) Construct-X EDC Developed externally on Tractus-X EDC. Semiconductor-X none yet Named in the ADR as a dataspace that needs a connector without Catena-X specifics. Any other dataspace that speaks DSP and uses DCP for authorization Tractus-X EDC with your extensions Possible today: write your rules as extensions, see Create a dataspace extension.

Only the Catena-X flavour is part of the Tractus-X release for now. Flavours for other dataspaces are built and released by those dataspaces, and may join the Tractus-X release later (the ADR leaves that open).

docs.title: Core and flavours
docs.text:
The ADR sorts every extension into one of three groups:

Group Meaning Examples today Generic (core) Works in any dataspace agreements, edr, tokenrefresh-handler, event-subscriber, tx-dcp Dataspace specific Only for one dataspace; prefixed with it, such as cx- for Catena-X cx-policy, cx-policy-legacy, cx-dcp, cx-connector-discovery, cx-dataspace-protocol, bdrs-client, bpn-validation, agreements-bpns Generic, but specific A generic need with a Catena-X implementation, to be split into the two groups above migrations (still to do); dcp, connector-discovery and dataspace-protocol are already split

The runtimes follow later: today the edc-controlplane-base and edc-dataplane-base runtimes are the Catena-X flavour. The ADR sketches a future layout with edc-controlplane-core and one module per flavour (edc-controlplane-catena-x, edc-controlplane-factory-x, …). Existing image, chart and Maven names stay as long as possible, so the change is silent for Catena-X users.

flowchart TB
  subgraph upstream["Eclipse Dataspace Components (upstream)"]
    edc["Connector framework · DSP · DCP"]
  end
  subgraph core["Tractus-X EDC core (dataspace agnostic)"]
    gen["agreements · EDR API · token refresh · DCP core · DSP versions"]
  end
  subgraph flavours["Dataspace flavours"]
    cx["Catena-X<br/>cx-policy · cx-dcp · BDRS · BPN"]
    fx["Factory-X<br/>external, PoC"]
    kx["Construct-X<br/>external"]
    yx["Your dataspace<br/>your extensions"]
  end
  edc --> core
  core --> cx
  core --> fx
  core --> kx
  core --> yx
  style core fill:#b8860b33,stroke:#b8860b

docs.title: Where new work happens
docs.text:
• Refactoring of existing extensions (splitting generic from Catena-X code) happens in this repository.
  • New flavours and new dataspace extensions are developed outside first, in another repository of Eclipse Tractus-X or of the dataspace, open or closed source, and may be merged here once they reach production status.

To start one, read Create a dataspace extension and come to the Connector Open Meeting.

docs.title: Create a dataspace extension
docs.text:
Every dataspace has its own rules: which credentials prove membership, which policy constraints partners may use, how participants are identified. In Tractus-X EDC these rules are extensions. The Catena-X rules are the cx-* extensions; this page shows how to write the same for another dataspace, called Example-X here.

Read Supported dataspaces first for the core and flavour model, and Tutorial 4: your first extension if you have never written an EDC extension.

docs.title: 1. What a dataspace usually adds
docs.text:
Rule of the dataspace Extension point Catena-X counterpart Policy constraints (membership, framework agreements, usage purposes) Policy functions on the PolicyEngine, bound with the RuleBindingRegistry cx-policy Credentials to request from a partner ScopeExtractor registered with the ScopeExtractorRegistry cx-dcp Credentials requested on every call Default scopes, a post-validator on the request policy contexts cx-dcp (CxDcpDefaultScopeExtension) Participant identifiers other than the DID An identity mapper such as a directory client bdrs-client, bpn-validation JSON-LD vocabulary for policies A JSON-LD context cached in the runtime core/json-ld-cx

Keep anything that every dataspace needs out of your extension and in the generic core, so it can be shared.

docs.title: 2. Create the module
docs.text:
Name the module after the dataspace, the way Catena-X uses cx-: for example ex-policy. Develop it in your own repository first; the ADR brings new flavours into this repository once they reach production status.

build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    `java-library`
}

dependencies {
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:boot-spi:<edc-version>")                    // ServiceExtension
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:runtime-metamodel:<edc-version>")           // @Extension, @Inject
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:policy-engine-spi:<edc-version>")           // PolicyEngine, rule functions
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:participant-spi:<edc-version>")             // ParticipantAgentPolicyContext
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:catalog-spi:<edc-version>")                 // CatalogPolicyContext
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:contract-spi:<edc-version>")                // negotiation and transfer contexts
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:request-policy-context-spi:<edc-version>")  // RequestPolicyContext
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:decentralized-claims-spi:<edc-version>")    // ScopeExtractor
    implementation("org.eclipse.edc:verifiable-credentials-spi:<edc-version>")  // VerifiableCredential
}

Use the EDC version that the Tractus-X EDC release you build on pins (edc in gradle/libs.versions.toml).

docs.title: 3. A policy constraint
docs.text:
An Example-X membership constraint, https://w3id.org/example-x/policy/Membership eq active, that passes when the partner presented an ExampleXMembershipCredential:

public class ExampleXMembershipFunction<C extends ParticipantAgentPolicyContext>
        implements AtomicConstraintRuleFunction<Permission, C> {

    static final String CREDENTIAL_TYPE = "ExampleXMembershipCredential";

    @Override
    public boolean evaluate(Operator operator, Object rightValue, Permission rule, C context) {
        if (operator != Operator.EQ || !"active".equals(rightValue)) {
            context.reportProblem("Membership only supports 'eq active'");
            return false;
        }
        var credentials = context.participantAgent().getClaims().get("vc");   // (1)!
        return credentials instanceof List<?> list && list.stream()
                .filter(VerifiableCredential.class::isInstance)
                .map(VerifiableCredential.class::cast)
                .anyMatch(vc -> vc.getType().contains(CREDENTIAL_TYPE));
    }
}
  1. The verified credentials of the partner, put there by the DCP extension after checking signatures, issuers and revocation.

Register it for the policy scopes in which it is evaluated (catalog, negotiation, transfer) and bind the constraint key to them, so that the engine evaluates it:

@Extension(ExampleXPolicyExtension.NAME)
public class ExampleXPolicyExtension implements ServiceExtension {

    static final String NAME = "Example-X policies";
    static final String MEMBERSHIP = "https://w3id.org/example-x/policy/Membership";

    @Inject
    private PolicyEngine policyEngine;

    @Inject
    private RuleBindingRegistry bindingRegistry;

    @Override
    public void initialize(ServiceExtensionContext context) {
        for (var scope : List.of("catalog", "contract.negotiation", "transfer.process")) {
            bindingRegistry.bind(MEMBERSHIP, scope);
        }
        policyEngine.registerFunction(CatalogPolicyContext.class, Permission.class, MEMBERSHIP,
                new ExampleXMembershipFunction<>());
        policyEngine.registerFunction(ContractNegotiationPolicyContext.class, Permission.class, MEMBERSHIP,
                new ExampleXMembershipFunction<>());
        policyEngine.registerFunction(TransferProcessPolicyContext.class, Permission.class, MEMBERSHIP,
                new ExampleXMembershipFunction<>());
    }
}

List the class in src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.eclipse.edc.spi.system.ServiceExtension, so the runtime finds it.

docs.title: 4. Ask for the right credentials
docs.text:
The provider can only evaluate the constraint if the consumer sends the credential. A ScopeExtractor tells the consumer's connector which DCP scope a policy needs:

public class ExampleXScopeExtractor implements ScopeExtractor {

    private static final String SCOPE_ALIAS = "org.example-x.vc.type";   // (1)!

    @Override
    public Set<String> extractScopes(Object leftValue, Operator operator, Object rightValue,
                                     RequestPolicyContext context) {
        return ExampleXPolicyExtension.MEMBERSHIP.equals(leftValue)
                ? Set.of(SCOPE_ALIAS + ":ExampleXMembershipCredential:read")
                : Set.of();
    }
}
  1. The scope alias your dataspace's wallets understand. Catena-X uses org.eclipse.tractusx.vc.type.

Register it in an extension with scopeExtractorRegistry.registerScopeExtractor(new ExampleXScopeExtractor()), as CxDcpScopeExtractorExtension does.

docs.title: 5. Build a runtime for your dataspace
docs.text:
An extension is active only in a runtime that has it on its classpath. Tractus-X EDC publishes its modules to Maven Central as org.eclipse.tractusx.edc:<module>:<version>. Until the ADR's core runtimes exist, start from the Catena-X runtimes and leave out the Catena-X modules you replace:

my-controlplane/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    runtimeOnly("org.eclipse.tractusx.edc:edc-controlplane-base:<tractusx-edc-version>") {
        exclude(group = "org.eclipse.tractusx.edc", module = "cx-policy")       // replaced by ex-policy
    }
    runtimeOnly(project(":ex-policy"))
}

Exclude carefully: other modules may depend on what you remove, so run the end-to-end tests of your runtime. The Factory-X EDC builds its runtimes this way and is a working example to learn from.

docs.title: 6. Test and share
docs.text:
• Unit-test each function with EDC's DependencyInjectionExtension, as in Testing.
  • Run two connectors of your flavour and negotiate a contract that uses your constraint.
  • Generic improvements you need on the way (a split of an extension that is still Catena-X specific) belong in this repository: open an issue or a pull request, see Contribution workflow.
  • Tell us about it: add your connector to Known friends and present it in the Connector Open Meeting.

docs.title: Deployment overview
docs.text: This section takes you from "I have nothing" to "my connector runs in production". Start with Deploy in five minutes below, then plan the real deployment with the rest of this page.

docs.title: Deploy in five minutes
docs.text:
Pick the variant that matches what you want to do. All four use the published Helm charts and Docker Hub images, so there is nothing to build. You need Docker, kind (or any other Kubernetes cluster), kubectl and Helm 3.

Try it (in memory)With PostgreSQL and VaultProductionFull dataspace (Umbrella)

One pod, everything in memory: the fastest way to see the Management API. For laptops only, it loses all data on restart.

# 1. A local Kubernetes cluster (skip if you already have one)
kind create cluster --name tractusx-edc

# 2. The Tractus-X Helm repository
helm repo add tractusx-edc https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev
helm repo update

# 3. Minimal values: dummy identity settings and a local API key
cat > edc-try.yaml <<'EOF'
fullnameOverride: tx-edc
participant:
  id: "did:web:changeme"
  bpnl: "BPNL000000000001"
  contextId: "try-participant-context"
dcp:
  sts:
    div:
      url: "https://div.example.org"
    oauth:
      token_url: "https://div.example.org/oauth/token"
      client:
        id: "try-client-id"
        secret_alias: "try-client-secret"
runtime:
  endpoints:
    management:
      authKey: password
  securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
  bdrs:
    server:
      url: "https://bdrs.example.org"
  token:
    signer:
      privatekey_alias: "key-1"
    verifier:
      publickey_alias: "key-1"
EOF

# 4. Install, then run the chart's own tests
helm install tx-edc tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector-memory -f edc-try.yaml --wait --timeout 5m
helm test tx-edc

Talk to the Management API:

kubectl port-forward deployment/tx-edc 8081:8081 &

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8081/management/v3/assets/request \
  -H "X-Api-Key: password" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"@context": {"@vocab": "https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/"}, "@type": "QuerySpec"}'

[] means the connector is up and you are authenticated. Clean up with kind delete cluster --name tractusx-edc.

The production chart: a control plane and a data plane, with a PostgreSQL and a dev-mode Vault installed next to them. Close to a real deployment, still with dummy identity settings.

kind create cluster --name tractusx-edc
helm repo add tractusx-edc https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev
helm repo update

cat > edc-local.yaml <<'EOF'
fullnameOverride: tx-edc
participant:
  id: "did:web:changeme"
  bpnl: "BPNL000000000001"
  contextId: "local-participant-context"
dcp:
  sts:
    div:
      url: "https://div.example.org"
    oauth:
      token_url: "https://div.example.org/oauth/token"
      client:
        id: "local-client-id"
        secret_alias: "client-secret"
controlplane:
  endpoints:
    management:
      authKey: password
  bdrs:
    server:
      url: "https://bdrs.example.org"
dataplane:
  token:
    signer:
      privatekey_alias: "key-1"
    verifier:
      publickey_alias: "key-1"
# install.postgresql and install.vault default to true: seed the dev Vault
vault:
  hashicorp:
    url: http://{{ .Release.Name }}-vault:8200
    token: root
  server:
    postStart:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |-
        {
        sleep 5
        /bin/vault kv put secret/client-secret content=kEmH7QRPWhKfy8f+x0pFMw==
        /bin/vault kv put secret/aes-keys content=YWVzX2VuY2tleV90ZXN0Cg==
        }
EOF

helm install tx-edc tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector -f edc-local.yaml --wait --timeout 10m
kubectl rollout status deployment tx-edc-controlplane
kubectl rollout status deployment tx-edc-dataplane
helm test tx-edc

The Management API is on the control plane: kubectl port-forward deployment/tx-edc-controlplane 8081:8081, then the same curl as in the first tab.

A real deployment uses your PostgreSQL, Vault, identity (DID, credential service, BDRS) and hostnames. Write them into a values file first: a minimal production values file is the starting point, and the checklist below lists what you need.

helm repo add tractusx-edc https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev
helm repo update
helm search repo tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector -l     # pick a released version

helm install my-connector tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace edc --create-namespace \
  -f my-values.yaml --wait --timeout 10m

helm test my-connector --namespace edc

Then work through the production checklist before you let partners in.

The Tractus-X Umbrella deploys a complete dataspace on one cluster: a provider and a consumer Tractus-X EDC, each with its own Tractus-X Identity Hub (DCP wallet with STS), an IssuerService that issues their credentials, and the BDRS. Since Umbrella release 25.12 this is its default setup.

git clone https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractus-x-umbrella.git
cd tractus-x-umbrella/charts/umbrella
helm dependency update
helm install -f values-adopter-decentralized-identityhub.yaml umbrella . \
  --namespace umbrella --create-namespace

Prepare the cluster (ingress, host names) with the Umbrella guide for Linux, macOS or Windows, then follow Data exchange with the Identity Hub for the participant DIDs and BPNs and a Bruno collection for the first exchange.

The first two variants cannot join a dataspace

Their DID, credential service and BDRS are placeholders. The connector starts, its APIs answer and the Helm tests pass, but it cannot negotiate with a real partner. For a complete local dataspace with two connectors and identity services, use the Umbrella tab above or the MXD tutorial. To run the charts with images you built yourself, follow the local quick start, which is the CI deployment test.

docs.title: What you deploy
docs.text:
Tractus-X EDC ships as container images and Helm charts. Pick the runtime that matches your goal:

Image (tractusx/… on Docker Hub) What it is Use it for edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault Control plane with PostgreSQL stores and HashiCorp Vault Production edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault Data plane with PostgreSQL and HashiCorp Vault Production edc-runtime-memory Control plane and data plane in one JVM, in-memory stores and vault Development and tests only Helm chart Deploys Use it for tractusx-connector A control plane and a data plane Deployment, optionally PostgreSQL and Vault as subcharts Production tractusx-connector-memory One Deployment running edc-runtime-memory Development and tests only

The in-memory runtime loses everything on restart

edc-runtime-memory keeps assets, contracts and secrets in memory, in plain text. It cannot run more than one replica. Never use it for real data.

Images are multi-architecture (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) and run as a non-root user. Charts are published to the Tractus-X Helm repository https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev.

docs.title: The production topology
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Internet
    partner[Partner connectors]
    consumerApp[Partner data consumers]
  end
  subgraph Your cluster
    direction LR
    ing[Ingress / Gateway<br/>TLS termination]
    cp[Control plane<br/>edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault]
    dp[Data plane<br/>edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault]
    ing -- "DSP /api/v1/dsp" --> cp
    ing -- "public /api/public" --> dp
    cp -- "control API" --> dp
    dp -- "registers via /v1/dataplanes" --> cp
  end
  subgraph Your platform
    pg[(PostgreSQL)]
    vault[(HashiCorp Vault)]
    apps[Your applications]
  end
  subgraph Dataspace services
    wallet[Credential service / DIV]
    bdrs[BDRS]
    issuer[Credential issuer]
  end
  partner --> ing
  consumerApp --> ing
  apps -- "Management API (internal only)" --> cp
  cp --> pg
  dp --> pg
  cp --> vault
  dp --> vault
  cp --> wallet
  cp --> bdrs
  wallet -.-> issuer

What this means for you:

  • Two public endpoints. Only the control plane's protocol (DSP) endpoint and the data plane's public endpoint face the internet.
  • Everything else stays internal. The Management API, the control API and the metrics port must never be reachable from outside.
  • Both planes need PostgreSQL and Vault. The data plane also has SQL stores and runs the database migrations.
  • Identity comes from outside. You need a DID, a DCP wallet with a Secure Token Service (STS) and the BDRS of your dataspace. Wallets in use with Tractus-X EDC are the open-source Tractus-X Identity Hub and SAP's managed Decentralized Identity Verification (DIV); any wallet that implements DCP works. See Identity and trust.

docs.title: Prerequisites checklist
docs.text:
Before you install the production chart, have these ready:

  • A Kubernetes cluster and Helm 3.
  • A PostgreSQL database (with a dedicated user) reachable from the cluster.
  • A HashiCorp Vault with a KV secrets engine and a token for the connector.
  • Your DID (participant.id) and BPNL (participant.bpnl).
  • A fresh, stable participant context id (a UUID). It must never change later.
  • OAuth client credentials for your credential service (STS/DIV) and the client secret stored in Vault.
  • The BDRS URL of your dataspace.
  • A key pair in Vault for signing and verifying data plane tokens.
  • Two hostnames with TLS certificates: one for the control plane protocol endpoint, one for the data plane public endpoint.
