docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A Tractus-X EDC runtime is configured through EDC settings: flat keys such as edc.participant.id or web.http.management.port. This page explains where settings come from, how they map to environment variables and Helm values, and how to pass secrets safely.

docs.title: Three ways to set a setting
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  helm[Helm values] -->|templates render| env[Environment variables]
  extra["controlplane.env /<br/>envValueFrom / envSecretNames"] --> env
  file["/app/configuration.properties"] --> rt[EDC runtime]
  env --> rt
  args["CLI args (e.g. --log-level)"] --> rt
  1. Environment variables. The usual way in Kubernetes. The name is the setting key in upper case, with . and - replaced by _: edc.participant.id → EDC_PARTICIPANT_ID.
  2. A properties file. The image starts Java with -Dedc.fs.config=/app/configuration.properties, so a mounted file at that path is read.
  3. Command-line arguments. The chart uses this for the log level (--log-level=INFO).

Every setting is declared in code with a @Setting annotation, which records its key, description and default. Each extension's README lists its settings.

docs.title: How Helm values become settings
docs.text:
The chart translates the documented values into environment variables. A few examples:

Helm value Environment variable Setting participant.id EDC_PARTICIPANT_ID, EDC_IAM_ISSUER_ID edc.participant.id, edc.iam.issuer.id participant.bpnl TRACTUSX_EDC_PARTICIPANT_BPN tractusx.edc.participant.bpn participant.contextId EDC_PARTICIPANT_CONTEXT_ID edc.participant.context.id controlplane.endpoints.management.authKey WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_KEY (with WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_TYPE=tokenbased) web.http.management.auth.key controlplane.endpoints.management.jwksUrl WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_DAC_KEY_URL (with …_AUTH_TYPE=delegated) web.http.management.auth.dac.key.url controlplane.bdrs.server.url TX_EDC_IAM_DCP_BDRS_SERVER_URL tx.edc.iam.dcp.bdrs.server.url dcp.sts.oauth.token_url EDC_IAM_STS_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL edc.iam.sts.oauth.token.url dcp.trustedIssuers[i] EDC_IAM_TRUSTED-ISSUER_<i>-ISSUER_ID edc.iam.trusted-issuer.<i>-issuer.id controlplane.policy.validation.enabled EDC_POLICY_VALIDATION_ENABLED edc.policy.validation.enabled vault.hashicorp.url, vault.hashicorp.token EDC_VAULT_HASHICORP_URL, EDC_VAULT_HASHICORP_TOKEN edc.vault.hashicorp.url, edc.vault.hashicorp.token dataplane.endpoints.proxy.authKey TX_EDC_DPF_CONSUMER_PROXY_AUTH_APIKEY tx.edc.dpf.consumer.proxy.auth.apikey dataplane.token.refresh.expiry_seconds TX_EDC_DATAPLANE_TOKEN_EXPIRY tx.edc.dataplane.token.expiry

The templates are the source of truth: deployment-controlplane.yaml and deployment-dataplane.yaml.

docs.title: Setting anything the chart does not expose
docs.text:
Each plane (controlplane, dataplane, and runtime in the memory chart) accepts:

Value Renders as Use it for env: {NAME: value} plain env entries Non-secret settings envValueFrom: {NAME: {secretKeyRef: …}} env with valueFrom Secrets, one key at a time envSecretNames: [secret] envFrom.secretRef A whole Secret of environment variables envConfigMapNames: [configmap] envFrom.configMapRef A whole ConfigMap of environment variables volumes, volumeMounts pod volumes Files such as certificates or a properties file initContainers init containers Preparation steps

Top-level customCaCerts adds your own CA certificates to the Java truststore.

docs.title: Passing secrets safely
docs.text:
The chart passes some sensitive values as plain environment values taken from values.yaml:

  • the Management API key (WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_KEY);
  • the consumer proxy API key (TX_EDC_DPF_CONSUMER_PROXY_AUTH_APIKEY);
  • the Vault token (EDC_VAULT_HASHICORP_TOKEN);
  • the AWS secret access key;
  • the database password, when you bring your own database.

For production, keep them out of your values files and override the variables from Kubernetes Secrets. Environment variables from envValueFrom are rendered after the chart's own, and Kubernetes uses the last definition of a duplicated name:

controlplane:
  envValueFrom:
    WEB_HTTP_MANAGEMENT_AUTH_KEY:
      secretKeyRef: {name: edc-secrets, key: management-api-key}
    EDC_VAULT_HASHICORP_TOKEN:
      secretKeyRef: {name: edc-secrets, key: vault-token}
    EDC_DATASOURCE_DEFAULT_PASSWORD:
      secretKeyRef: {name: edc-db, key: password}

Check the result

Run helm template with your values and inspect the rendered env list before you install. Kubernetes accepts duplicated names, uses the last one and prints a warning; some GitOps tools reject duplicates. Note that envSecretNames and envConfigMapNames cannot override the chart's variables, because explicit env entries always win over envFrom.

The chart marks these values as required, so keep a non-empty placeholder in your values file when you override them from a Secret.

Everything else that is secret (the STS client secret, token signing keys, data source credentials of assets) lives in Vault and is referenced by an alias.

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning edc.datasource.default.url, .user, .password – The default data source used by all stores. edc.sql.store.<store>.datasource default Use a different data source for one store. tx.edc.postgresql.migration.enabled true Run the Flyway schema migrations at startup. tx.edc.postgresql.migration.schema public Schema the migrations run in.

See Persistence and state for how migrations work.

docs.title: Look up a setting
docs.text:
To find a setting's key, environment variable, Helm value, documentation and history in one go, use the setting-lifecycle skill of the Connector Sensei:

.claude/skills/setting-lifecycle/scripts/setting-trace.sh tx.edc.iam.dcp.bdrs.server.url

docs.title: Helm chart
docs.text: The tractusx-connector chart deploys a control plane and a data plane. This page explains the values you will touch in almost every installation. For the complete, generated list of every value and its default, see the chart README: charts/tractusx-connector/README.md.

docs.title: Install from the Tractus-X Helm repository
docs.text:
helm repo add tractusx-edc https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev
helm repo update
helm search repo tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector -l   # list the available versions

helm install my-connector tractusx-edc/tractusx-connector \
  --version <chart-version> \
  -f my-values.yaml

docs.title: A minimal production values file
docs.text:
The example below assumes an existing PostgreSQL and Vault. Every CHANGEME-style default must be replaced.

my-values.yaml
install:
  postgresql: false            # bring your own database
  vault: false                 # bring your own Vault

participant:
  id: "did:web:connector.example.com"      # your DID
  bpnl: "BPNL000000000001"                 # your BPNL
  contextId: "5b9e7e4e-…"                  # generate once, never change

dcp:
  trustedIssuers:
    - "did:web:issuer.example.org"         # DID of the credential issuer of your dataspace
  sts:
    oauth:
      token_url: "https://div.example.org/oauth/token"
      client:
        id: "my-client-id"
        secret_alias: "client-secret"      # Vault key holding the client secret

controlplane:
  endpoints:
    management:
      authKey: "set-from-secret"           # placeholder, overridden from a Secret (see "Configuration")
  bdrs:
    server:
      url: "https://bdrs.example.org/api/directory"
  ingresses:
    - enabled: true                        # public: DSP protocol endpoint only
      hostname: "edc-control.example.com"
      endpoints: [protocol]
      className: nginx
      tls:
        enabled: true
  logs:
    level: INFO

dataplane:
  token:
    signer:
      privatekey_alias: "tx-token-signer"      # Vault key: private key for signing EDR tokens
    verifier:
      publickey_alias: "tx-token-verifier"     # Vault key: matching public key
  ingresses:
    - enabled: true                        # public: data plane public API only
      hostname: "edc-data.example.com"
      endpoints: [public]
      className: nginx
      tls:
        enabled: true
  logs:
    level: INFO

postgresql:
  jdbcUrl: "jdbc:postgresql://<postgres-host>:5432/edc"
  # credentials: see "Configuration" for passing them as Secrets

vault:
  hashicorp:
    url: "https://vault.example.com"
    # token: see "Configuration" for passing it as a Secret

Hostnames decide the URLs your partners see

The DSP callback address and the data plane public URL are derived from the first ingress of each plane, and switch to https:// when that ingress has tls.enabled: true. To set them explicitly, use controlplane.url.protocol and dataplane.url.public.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Value Default Meaning participant.id did:web:changeme Your connector's DID. Since 0.13 this is the DID, not the BPNL. participant.bpnl BPNLCHANGEME Your BPNL. participant.contextId UUID CHANGEME Participant context id. Used as a key in the database. Never change it once set. dcp.trustedIssuers [] DIDs of trusted credential issuers. Each entry is a string or {id, supportedTypes}. dcp.sts.oauth.token_url, dcp.sts.oauth.client.id, dcp.sts.oauth.client.secret_alias CHANGEME OAuth client for the STS/DIV. The secret itself is read from Vault under the alias. dcp.sts.div.url empty Base URL of the DIV, if used. dcp.cache.enabled, dcp.cache.validity true, 86400 Cache for verifiable presentations (seconds). controlplane.bdrs.server.url CHANGEME BDRS base URL.

docs.title: Security of the APIs
docs.text: Value Default Meaning controlplane.endpoints.management.authKey password Value of the X-Api-Key header for the Management API. controlplane.endpoints.management.jwksUrl empty If set, the Management API uses delegated (JWT) authentication instead of the API key. dataplane.endpoints.proxy.authKey password API key of the consumer proxy API. dataplane.token.signer.privatekey_alias, dataplane.token.verifier.publickey_alias CHANGEME Vault aliases of the key pair that signs and verifies data plane access tokens. controlplane.policy.validation.enabled true Reject policies that do not follow the Catena-X policy rules. See Catena-X policies.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Value Default Meaning install.postgresql, install.vault true, true Install PostgreSQL and Vault as subcharts. Set both to false for production. postgresql.jdbcUrl jdbc:postgresql://{{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql:5432/edc Used when install.postgresql is false. vault.hashicorp.url, vault.hashicorp.token http://{{ .Release.Name }}-vault:8200, root Vault address and token. vault.hashicorp.paths.secret, vault.hashicorp.paths.folder /v1/secret, empty KV path and an optional folder for all keys. networkPolicy.enabled false Create ingress-only NetworkPolicies for both planes.

The bundled Vault is a dev-mode Vault

With install.vault: true the chart installs Vault in dev mode with root token root, and the bundled PostgreSQL has persistence disabled. Both are for tests only.

docs.title: Ports and paths
docs.text:
Plane Endpoint Port Path Exposure Control plane default (health checks) 8080 /api internal Control plane management 8081 /management internal only, never on the internet Control plane control 8083 /control internal (data plane ↔ control plane) Control plane protocol (DSP) 8084 /api/v1/dsp public Control plane metrics 9090 /metrics internal Data plane default (health checks) 8080 /api internal Data plane public 8081 /api/public public Data plane control 8084 /api/control internal Data plane proxy (consumer proxy) 8186 /proxy internal Data plane metrics 9090 /metrics internal

Health probes call GET /api/check/liveness and GET /api/check/readiness on the default port.

Changing the proxy port

The chart does not pass the proxy port to the runtime, which listens on its built-in default 8186. If you change dataplane.endpoints.proxy.port, also set TX_EDC_DPF_CONSUMER_PROXY_PORT in dataplane.env.

docs.title: Exposing the endpoints
docs.text:
Each plane has a list of ingresses (Kubernetes Ingress) and of httpRoutes (Gateway API). Each entry chooses which endpoints it exposes. The chart defaults are already split the right way, but disabled:

  • controlplane.ingresses[0]: public, exposes protocol.
  • controlplane.ingresses[1]: intranet, exposes management and control.
  • dataplane.ingresses[0]: public, exposes public.

Each entry supports className, tls.enabled, tls.secretName and cert-manager annotations through certManager.issuer or certManager.clusterIssuer.

docs.title: Resources and scaling
docs.text:
Value Default *.resources.requests cpu: 500m, memory: 1024Mi *.resources.limits cpu: 1.5, memory: 1024Mi *.replicaCount 1 *.autoscaling.enabled false

Autoscaling template uses a removed API

The HPA templates use autoscaling/v2beta1, which current Kubernetes versions no longer serve. Until the chart is updated, scale with replicaCount instead of autoscaling.enabled.

With more than one control plane replica (or autoscaling), the chart disables DID service self-deregistration automatically.

docs.title: The in-memory chart
docs.text: tractusx-connector-memory runs one edc-runtime-memory pod. Its values live under runtime.* instead of controlplane.*/dataplane.*, it has no PostgreSQL or Vault, and secrets are seeded with vault.secrets (key1:secret1;key2:secret2). See charts/tractusx-connector-memory/README.md.

docs.title: Local quick start (kind)
docs.text:
In this guide you build the images, install the production chart on a local kind cluster with PostgreSQL and Vault, and check that the connector is healthy. The steps follow the repository's own deployment test (.github/actions/run-deployment-test/action.yml and .github/workflows/deployment-test.yaml), so they are exercised on every CI run.

What you get, and what you don't

The test values use dummy identity settings (DID, STS, BDRS). The connector starts, its APIs answer and the Helm tests pass, but it cannot talk to a real dataspace. For a complete local dataspace with two connectors and identity services, use the MXD tutorial.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Tool Version used in CI JDK 21 Docker any recent version kind v0.32.0 or newer (needed for current kindest/node images) kubectl v1.31 or newer Helm v3.16 or newer

docs.title: 1. Create the cluster
docs.text: kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.36.1

docs.title: 2. Build the images
docs.text:
From the repository root:

./gradlew -p edc-controlplane/edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault dockerize
./gradlew -p edc-dataplane/edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault dockerize

Each dockerize call builds a shadow jar and a local image tagged <module>:latest and <module>:<version>.

docs.title: 3. Load the images into kind
docs.text:
kind load docker-image \
  edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault:latest \
  edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault:latest

docs.title: 4. Install the chart
docs.text:
helm install tx-prod charts/tractusx-connector \
  -f edc-tests/deployment/src/main/resources/helm/tractusx-connector-test.yaml \
  --dependency-update --wait-for-jobs --timeout=120s

kubectl rollout status deployment tx-prod-controlplane
kubectl rollout status deployment tx-prod-dataplane

The test values file (tractusx-connector-test.yaml):

  • uses the local images (pullPolicy: Never, tag latest);
  • keeps the chart defaults install.postgresql: true and install.vault: true, so a PostgreSQL and a dev-mode Vault are installed next to the connector;
  • seeds the Vault with the secrets the connector expects (client-secret, aes-keys) in a postStart hook;
  • uses dummy DID, BPN, STS and BDRS values.

docs.title: 5. Run the Helm tests
docs.text:
helm test tx-prod

The chart's tests check that:

  1. the data plane answers GET /api/check/readiness;
  2. the Management API accepts a request with the API key (POST /management/v3/business-partner-groups);
  3. the Management API rejects a request without the API key.

docs.title: 6. Talk to the Management API
docs.text:
kubectl port-forward deployment/tx-prod-controlplane 8081:8081 &

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8081/management/v3/assets/request \
  -H "X-Api-Key: password" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"@context": {"@vocab": "https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/"}, "@type": "QuerySpec"}'

An empty JSON array [] means the connector is up and you are authenticated. password is the chart default for controlplane.endpoints.management.authKey. Never keep it outside your laptop.

Continue with Tutorial 1: your first data exchange to create an asset and an offer.

docs.title: Even simpler: the in-memory chart
docs.text:
To try the API without PostgreSQL and Vault, use the in-memory runtime, again as CI does:

./gradlew -p edc-controlplane/edc-runtime-memory dockerize
kind load docker-image edc-runtime-memory:latest

helm install tx-inmem charts/tractusx-connector-memory \
  -f edc-tests/deployment/src/main/resources/helm/tractusx-connector-memory-test.yaml \
  --wait-for-jobs --timeout=120s --dependency-update
kubectl rollout status deployment tx-inmem
helm test tx-inmem

Secrets for the in-memory vault are seeded with the vault.secrets value, in the form key1:secret1;key2:secret2.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
helm uninstall tx-prod tx-inmem
kind delete cluster

docs.title: Without Kubernetes
docs.text: Each runtime is a plain Java application (main class org.eclipse.edc.boot.system.runtime.BaseRuntime). The image entrypoint reads settings from /app/configuration.properties and from environment variables, so you can also use docker run with a mounted properties file. See the README of each runtime module for an example: memory runtime, control plane, data plane. The ports a runtime listens on are whatever you configure in the web.http.* settings; the chart defaults are listed in Helm chart.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
Tractus-X EDC runs wherever Kubernetes or a container runtime runs: the tractusx-connector Helm chart and the images on Docker Hub make no assumption about a cloud. This page shows what to use from each platform, and points to the projects that already deploy the connector there.

Every production setup needs the same four things, whatever the platform:

Need Chart setting Bring your own PostgreSQL install.postgresql: false, postgresql.jdbcUrl, postgresql.auth A managed PostgreSQL A HashiCorp Vault compatible secret store install.vault: false, vault.hashicorp.url, vault.hashicorp.token HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao Ingresses with TLS for the DSP and public data plane endpoints controlplane.ingresses, dataplane.ingresses An ingress controller and certificates A DCP wallet dcp.* Tractus-X Identity Hub, SAP DIV or another wallet

The bundled PostgreSQL and Vault (in dev mode, root token root) are for tests only. Work through the production checklist and tune for production on any platform.

docs.title: Amazon Web Services
docs.text:
Building block AWS service Kubernetes Amazon EKS PostgreSQL Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL or Aurora PostgreSQL Secrets HashiCorp Vault on EKS or HCP Vault (the standard images read secrets from a HashiCorp Vault API) Ingress AWS Load Balancer Controller, certificates from ACM Data Amazon S3 with the built-in AmazonS3-PUSH transfer Access to S3 without keys IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) or EKS Pod Identity on the data plane's service account

Projects to start from:

  • Dataspace Connector on AWS

    The dataspace connector of AWS Labs, built on the Tractus-X EDC control plane and data plane runtimes, with its own AWS integrations.

    awslabs/dataspace-connector-on-aws

  • AWS EDC pattern

    Terraform, Kubernetes and Helm patterns by Think-iT that install the tractusx-connector chart on EKS.

    Think-iT-Labs/aws-patterns-edc

values-aws.yaml (excerpt)
install:
  postgresql: false
  vault: false
postgresql:
  # Replace ${RDS_ENDPOINT} with the endpoint of your RDS instance.
  jdbcUrl: "jdbc:postgresql://${RDS_ENDPOINT}:5432/edc"
vault:
  hashicorp:
    url: "https://vault.example.com"
serviceAccount:
  create: true
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/edc-dataplane-s3"   # IRSA

docs.title: Microsoft Azure
docs.text:
Building block Azure service Kubernetes Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) PostgreSQL Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server Secrets HashiCorp Vault on AKS or HCP Vault Ingress Application Gateway for Containers, or NGINX ingress with cert-manager Data Azure Blob Storage with the built-in AzureStorage-PUSH transfer

No Azure Key Vault distribution

Until 0.8, Tractus-X EDC also shipped images and a chart with Azure Key Vault. They were deprecated in 0.8.0 and are no longer published since 0.9.0, so that the project maintains one distribution built on open-source services (ADR). If you need Key Vault, build your own runtime with the upstream vault extension; see Writing extensions.

docs.title: Other Kubernetes platforms
docs.text: The chart is plain Kubernetes, so Google Kubernetes Engine, Red Hat OpenShift, SUSE Rancher, STACKIT, IONOS, Open Telekom Cloud and on-premises clusters work the same way: a managed or self-run PostgreSQL, a HashiCorp Vault compatible store and an ingress controller. On OpenShift, check that the pod security settings of the chart (*.securityContext) fit your security context constraints.

docs.title: Local and test setups
docs.text:
Setup For Guide kind One connector on your machine, from source Local quick start Tractus-X Umbrella A full dataspace: two connectors, Identity Hubs, BDRS and more Deploy in five minutes Docker Compose Two connectors without Kubernetes Home: install, Tractus-X Starter Kit EDC Management Console Provisioning connectors from a web UI ARENA2036/edc-management-console

Platform guides to come

Step-by-step guides per platform are planned. If you run Tractus-X EDC on a platform and want to share how, open a pull request or present it in the Connector Open Meeting, and add your project to Known friends.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
The chart defaults are chosen so that helm install works out of the box on a laptop. They are not secure enough for production. Go through this list before you connect a connector to a live dataspace.

The defaults are for development

The bundled Vault runs in dev mode with the root token root, and the bundled PostgreSQL has no persistence. Restarting a pod can lose all your agreements and keys.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• External PostgreSQL. Set install.postgresql: false and point postgresql.jdbcUrl, postgresql.auth.username and postgresql.auth.password to a managed, backed-up database. Use a dedicated user rather than an admin user (see the chart's database configuration).
  • External Vault. Set install.vault: false and configure vault.hashicorp.url and a token with a narrow policy. Avoid HashiCorp Vault 1.18.1, which has a known path-handling bug.
  • Persistent identities. Set participant.id (your DID), participant.bpnl and participant.contextId. Never change participant.contextId after the first start: it is written into the migrated data.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• Do not put secrets in values.yaml. The chart renders these as plain environment values: the management API key, the consumer proxy API key, the Vault token, the AWS secret key and the database password (when you use an external database). Store them in Kubernetes Secrets and inject them with controlplane.envValueFrom / dataplane.envValueFrom, as shown in Configuration → secrets.
  • Strong management API credentials. Replace the default authKey, or better, switch to delegated auth by setting controlplane.endpoints.management.jwksUrl so that the API accepts JWTs from your identity provider.
  • Vault aliases are filled. dcp.sts.oauth.client.secret_alias, dataplane.token.signer.privatekey_alias and dataplane.token.verifier.publickey_alias must name existing Vault entries.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• Expose only what partners need. Only the protocol (DSP) endpoint of the control plane and the public endpoint of the data plane must be reachable from the internet. Keep management, control and proxy internal.
  • TLS on every public ingress. Set tls.enabled: true and either tls.secretName or a cert-manager issuer / clusterIssuer. The chart switches the advertised DSP and public URLs to https:// only when the first ingress has TLS enabled.
  • NetworkPolicy. Enable networkPolicy.enabled: true and restrict networkPolicy.controlplane.from / networkPolicy.dataplane.from. The default namespaceSelector: {} allows every namespace.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
• Trusted issuers. Configure dcp.trustedIssuers with the DIDs of the issuers your dataspace trusts.
  • BDRS. In Catena-X, set controlplane.bdrs.server.url to the BDRS of the dataspace.
  • Policy validation stays on. Keep controlplane.policy.validation.enabled: true (the default) so that malformed Catena-X policies are rejected when they are created.

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
• Log level. The chart default is DEBUG. Set controlplane.logs.level / dataplane.logs.level to INFO.
  • Resources. Defaults are requests 500m / 1024Mi and limits 1.5 CPU / 1024Mi. Size them from your load tests.
  • Read-only root filesystem. It is enabled by default and /tmp is writable. If you use multipart uploads and see write errors, check the temp directory before you relax this setting.
  • Autoscaling. The HPA templates use autoscaling/v2beta1, which current Kubernetes versions no longer serve. Check this before you set autoscaling.enabled: true; scale with replicaCount instead. More than one replica also turns off DID self-deregistration.
  • Upgrades rehearsed. Read Upgrades and run the upgrade on a staging copy of your database.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
helm test <release>                    # runs the chart's built-in test
kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=<release>
curl -s https://<public-host>/api/v1/dsp/.well-known/dspace-version   # DSP version discovery

docs.title: How Tractus-X EDC is released
docs.text:
Cadence Quarterly, aligned with Tractus-X releases Version scheme Minor version per release (0.12.0, 0.13.0, …). Breaking changes are possible between minor versions. Bugfix releases (0.13.1) contain only fixes. Support Only the latest release is maintained, and only for critical functional or security issues. Fixes are not backported. Pre-releases Release candidates X.Y.Z-rcN; dated snapshots X.Y.Z-YYYYMMDD-SNAPSHOT Release notes GitHub Releases Artifacts Docker images on Docker Hub (tractusx/…), Helm charts at https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/charts/dev, Maven artifacts on Maven Central

The decisions behind this are recorded in the ADRs release train, improvements to the versioning scheme and release process.

docs.title: Upgrade in five steps
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  a[1. Read every migration guide<br/>between your versions] --> b[2. Back up database<br/>and Vault]
  b --> c[3. Update values<br/>renamed / removed settings]
  c --> d[4. helm upgrade<br/>on staging]
  d --> e[5. Verify, then production]
  1. Read the migration guides. Do not skip versions when you read them: each guide describes only the step from the previous minor version. They are listed in the migration guides section.
  2. Back up the PostgreSQL database and the Vault secrets.
  3. Update your values. Migration guides list renamed Helm values and settings. An unknown setting is silently ignored, so check carefully.

  4. Upgrade.

    helm repo update tractusx
helm upgrade <release> tractusx/tractusx-connector --version <new-version> -f my-values.yaml

    The database schema is migrated automatically at startup by Flyway (see Persistence). 5. Verify with helm test <release> and a catalog request to a known partner.

CI checks on every change that an in-place helm upgrade from the latest released chart to the current chart works (.github/workflows/upgradeability-test.yaml).

docs.title: Highlights of recent releases
docs.text:
0.12 → 0.13
  • participant.id now holds your DID. The BPNL moved to participant.bpnl.
  • iatp.* values were renamed to dcp.*, and DIM to DIV (Decentralized Identity Verifier).
  • The Federated Catalog was removed.
  • The bundled PostgreSQL moved from Bitnami to CloudPirates charts and PostgreSQL 18. This cannot be upgraded in place; follow the generic PostgreSQL migration guide.
  • Per-store data source names now use edc.sql.store.<store>.datasource.

Full guide: 0.12.x → 0.13.x

0.11 → 0.12

Full guide: 0.11.x → 0.12.x

docs.title: Upgrading the upstream EDC (for maintainers)
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC pins one upstream Eclipse EDC version in gradle/libs.versions.toml. Bumping it is described in the upstream-edc-bump skill of the Connector Sensei.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
You want to change the connector itself: fix a bug, add a feature, write an extension. This section takes you from a fresh clone to a merged pull request.

  • Setup

    Toolchain, build commands, IDE code style, running a runtime locally.

docs.title: The shortest path
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc.git
cd tractusx-edc
./gradlew build                     # compile, unit tests, Checkstyle

Then pick a good first issue and read Contributing.

docs.title: Code architecture
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC is a distribution of Eclipse EDC. Most of the connector comes from upstream EDC modules; this repository adds Tractus-X and Catena-X extensions and assembles them into runnable runtimes.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path What lives there spi/ Tractus-X service provider interfaces: core-spi, edr-spi, bdrs-client-spi, dcp-spi, tokenrefresh-spi, … core/ Shared libraries: edr-core, json-ld-core, json-ld-cx, core-utils edc-extensions/ All Tractus-X extensions (policies, BPN validation, EDR API, DCP, DSP 0.8, data plane proxy, migrations, …) edc-controlplane/ Control plane runtimes: edc-controlplane-base, edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault, edc-runtime-memory edc-dataplane/ Data plane runtimes: edc-dataplane-base, edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault edc-tests/ End-to-end suites, fixtures, compatibility tests, test runtimes, deployment test values charts/ Helm charts tractusx-connector and tractusx-connector-memory docs/ This documentation, the Management API walkthrough, ADRs and migration guides resources/ Checkstyle, license headers, IDE code style, the runtime Dockerfile, docs tooling gradle/libs.versions.toml Version catalog, including the pinned upstream edc version .claude/, .github/agents/ The Connector Sensei agent and its skills

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  R1[edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault] --> CPB[edc-controlplane-base]
  R2[edc-runtime-memory] --> CPB
  R2 --> DPB[edc-dataplane-base]
  R3[edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault] --> DPB
  R1 --> SQL[SQL stores + connector-migration]
  R3 --> MIG[connector-migration]
  CPB --> EXT[edc-extensions/*]
  DPB --> EXT
  EXT --> CORE[core/*]
  EXT --> SPI[spi/*]
  CORE --> SPI
  CPB -. BOMs .-> UP[(Upstream EDC modules)]
  DPB -. BOMs .-> UP
  SPI --> USPI[(Upstream EDC SPIs)]
  • SPIs contain interfaces and model classes only. They depend on other SPIs and libraries.
  • Core libraries implement shared logic on top of SPIs.
  • Extensions depend on SPIs and core libraries, never on each other's implementation classes. They find each other at runtime through dependency injection.
  • Base runtimes (edc-controlplane-base, edc-dataplane-base) are plain dependency lists: upstream BOMs plus the Tractus-X extensions, minus a few upstream modules that Tractus-X replaces.
  • Distributions add persistence (SQL stores, Flyway) and secrets (HashiCorp Vault), and build a fat jar and a Docker image.

docs.title: How a runtime is composed
docs.text:
There is no "main application code". A runtime is its classpath:

sequenceDiagram
  participant Boot as BaseRuntime (upstream)
  participant SL as ServiceLoader
  participant Ext as Extensions
  Boot->>SL: load all ServiceExtension classes (META-INF/services)
  Boot->>Boot: build dependency graph from @Inject / @Provider
  Boot->>Ext: initialize() in dependency order
  Boot->>Ext: prepare()
  Boot->>Ext: start()
  Note over Ext: web contexts, state machines and schedulers run

Consequences you will meet as a developer:

  • To ship a feature, add its module to a base runtime's build.gradle.kts.
  • To replace an upstream module, exclude it in the base runtime and provide your own. For example, edc-controlplane-base excludes upstream edr-cache-api (replaced by edr-api-v2) and the remote STS client (replaced by tx-dcp-sts-div).
  • Default implementations use @Provider(isDefault = true). A SQL store on the classpath replaces the in-memory default automatically.

docs.title: What each runtime contains
docs.text:
Control planeData planeIn-memory

edc-controlplane-base = upstream control plane base + DCP BOMs, plus:

Area Tractus-X modules Policies cx-policy, cx-policy-legacy, bpn-validation, validators/* Identity dcp/{cx-dcp, tx-dcp, tx-dcp-sts-div, verifiable-presentation-cache}, bdrs-client, did-document/* Protocol dataspace-protocol, dsp/*-08 (DSP 0.8 backport), token-interceptor EDR edr/{edr-api-v2, edr-callback}, tokenrefresh-handler, core:edr-core Agreements agreements, agreements-bpns Discovery connector-discovery/* Misc log4j2-monitor, event-subscriber, data-flow-properties-provider

The PostgreSQL distribution adds the SQL stores retirement-evaluation-store-sql, bpns-evaluation-store-sql, business-partner-store-sql, edr-index-lock-sql and migrations:connector-migration.

edc-dataplane-base = upstream data plane base BOM, plus:

Area Tractus-X modules Proxy dataplane-proxy/{dataplane-proxy-http, dataplane-public-api-v2, edc-dataplane-proxy-consumer-api} Token refresh dataplane-token-refresh/{token-refresh-api, token-refresh-core}, tokenrefresh-handler Data flows dataflow/{dataflow-api, dataflow-service}, non-finite-provider-push-core Identity dcp:tx-dcp-sts-div

Upstream modules add S3 and Azure Blob transfers, DID resolution and the EDR store.

edc-runtime-memory = edc-controlplane-base + edc-dataplane-base in one process, with in-memory stores and a vault seeded from tx.edc.vault.secrets. For development and tests only.

docs.title: Where to look for…
docs.text:
I want to understand… Start here A Catena-X policy constraint edc-extensions/cx-policy/src/main/java/org/eclipse/tractusx/edc/policy/cx/ Credential scopes and VP handling edc-extensions/dcp/ The EDR API edc-extensions/edr/edr-api-v2/ Token refresh on the provider edc-extensions/dataplane/dataplane-token-refresh/ A database table edc-extensions/migrations/connector-migration/src/main/resources/migrations/connector/ A setting grep -rn '"<key>"' --include=*.java . or the setting-lifecycle skill Upstream behaviour the edc-upstream-sources skill, at the pinned version

The full module list is in the extension catalogue.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC is an Eclipse Foundation project. Contributions are welcome from everyone who follows a few rules.

docs.title: Before your first contribution
docs.text:
1. Sign the Eclipse Contributor Agreement with the e-mail address you use for your commits. Without an ECA, a pull request cannot be merged.
  2. Talk first. Open an issue or a discussion describing what you want to change. Unannounced pull requests may be ignored.
  3. Read the PR etiquette, the style guide and the coding principles.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  i[Issue or discussion] --> f[Fork + branch]
  f --> c[Code + tests]
  c --> l[Local checks]
  l --> pr[Draft PR]
  pr --> r[Ready for review]
  r --> m[Squash merge by a committer]
  • Work in your fork and open the pull request against main.
  • Keep pull requests focused on one feature or bug.
  • The PR title is the commit message after the squash merge, and must follow Conventional Commits: <type>(<optional scope>): <description>, under 80 characters, with type build, chore, ci, docs, feat, fix, perf, refactor, revert, style or test. Example: feat(edr): add filter by provider to /v3/edrs/request.
  • Fill in the pull request template.
  • Mark the PR Ready for review only when you are done; reviewers aim to respond within two business days.

docs.title: Local checks before you push
docs.text:
./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest checkstyleTestFixtures   # Checkstyle errors fail CI
./gradlew test                                                   # unit tests
./gradlew -p edc-tests/e2e/<suite> test -DincludeTags="EndToEndTest"   # if behaviour changed
If you change… Also do A setting or Helm value Update the extension README, values.yaml, regenerate the chart README with helm-docs, and mention it in the migration guide The database schema Add a Flyway migration in edc-extensions/migrations/connector-migration An API Update the OpenAPI annotations and the Management API walkthrough A third-party dependency Run the Eclipse Dash license check (dependencies-and-dash skill) and mention the library in the PR Anything operators see Add an entry to the upcoming migration guide

The breaking-change-guard skill finds most of these follow-ups for you:

.claude/skills/breaking-change-guard/scripts/bc-scan.sh

docs.title: Licenses and headers
docs.text:
• Code is Apache-2.0, documentation CC-BY-4.0.
  • Every source file starts with the license header from resources/java.header or resources/hashtag.header. Checkstyle checks it.
  • AI-assisted contributions carry an AI disclosure and an Assisted-By: line, and must be reviewed and verified by the person who submits them. See the Connector Sensei for the exact format.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs Material from the docs/ folder and mkdocs.yml. Preview it locally:

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r resources/docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000/tractusx-edc/

Before you push, run mkdocs build --strict. CI runs it too. For a pull request from a branch of this repository that changes the documentation, it also publishes a preview at https://eclipse-tractusx.github.io/tractusx-edc/pr-preview/<number>/, links it in a comment on the pull request and removes it when the pull request is closed. Pull requests from forks are only built; download the site from the documentation-site artifact of the run. The site is published from main on every push that changes the documentation and by the release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) after each release. New pages must be added to nav in mkdocs.yml and end with the ## NOTICE section.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
Significant technical decisions are recorded as architecture decision records (ADRs) in docs/development/decision-records/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<title>/README.md, with the sections Decision, Rationale and Approach. Propose an ADR in its own pull request before you implement a larger change. The migration-guide-and-adr skill creates one in the house format.

All accepted decisions are listed in the decision record index.

docs.title: Writing extensions
docs.text: New to extensions? Do Tutorial 4 first. This page is the reference for the idioms used in this repository.

docs.title: Where does it belong?
docs.text:
Kind Location Example Generic, useful in any dataspace edc-extensions/<feature> agreements, event-subscriber Catena-X specific edc-extensions/cx-<feature>, or a cx- sibling module cx-policy, dcp/cx-dcp Contracts other modules use spi/<feature>-spi or edc-extensions/<feature>/<feature>-spi spi/edr-spi, bpn-validation/bpn-validation-spi Useful to all EDC users contribute to upstream EDC –

If a generic feature needs Catena-X behaviour, put the interface in the generic module and the Catena-X implementation in a cx- module, as dcp/tx-dcp and dcp/cx-dcp do. Rules of other dataspaces follow the same split: the generic module holds the interface, a dataspace-specific module the implementation (see Create a dataspace extension). Background: multi-dataspace support ADR.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
edc-extensions/my-feature/
├── build.gradle.kts
├── README.md                                      # purpose + settings table
└── src/main
    ├── java/org/eclipse/tractusx/edc/myfeature/MyFeatureExtension.java
    └── resources/META-INF/services/org.eclipse.edc.spi.system.ServiceExtension

Generate this with:

.claude/skills/new-extension/scripts/scaffold-extension.sh <dir> <java-package> <ClassName>Extension [setting.prefix]

docs.title: The annotations
docs.text:
@Extension(value = SqlAgreementsRetirementStoreExtension.NAME)
public class SqlAgreementsRetirementStoreExtension implements ServiceExtension {

    protected static final String NAME = "SQL Agreement Retirement Store.";

    @Setting(key = "tx.edc.sql.store.agreementretirement.datasource",
             description = "Datasource name for the SQL AgreementsRetirement store",
             defaultValue = DataSourceRegistry.DEFAULT_DATASOURCE)
    private String dataSourceName;

    @Inject
    private DataSourceRegistry dataSourceRegistry;

    @Inject(required = false)
    private SqlAgreementsRetirementStatements statements;

    @Provider
    public AgreementsRetirementStore sqlStore() {
        return new SqlAgreementsRetirementStore(dataSourceRegistry, dataSourceName, /* … */);
    }
}
Annotation Purpose @Extension Names the extension (used in logs and the dependency graph). @Setting Injects a configuration value. Always give description, and defaultValue when there is one. @Settings record + @Configuration field Groups related settings into a typed record. @Inject Gets a service from another extension. required = false makes it optional. @Provider Offers a service. isDefault = true marks a fallback that another provider may replace.

docs.title: Register, don't wire
docs.text:
Extensions contribute behaviour by registering it in upstream registries in initialize():

To add… Register with A policy function PolicyEngine.registerFunction(...) and RuleBindingRegistry.bind(...) A JSON-LD transformer TypeTransformerRegistry.register(...) A request validator JsonObjectValidatorRegistry.register(...) An HTTP controller WebService.registerResource(ApiContext.MANAGEMENT, controller)

Adding or versioning an HTTP endpoint is covered by the management-api-endpoint skill of the Connector Sensei.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Fail fast. Read and validate configuration in initialize().
  • No checked exceptions. Return Result / ServiceResult for expected failures; extend EdcException otherwise.
  • Secrets only in the Vault, and never in logs. Log through the injected Monitor.
  • JSON via TypeManager, not your own ObjectMapper.
  • Persistence: a …Statements interface, a PostgreSQL dialect, a data source @Setting, and a Flyway migration in connector-migration (see the sql-migration skill).
  • Settings that operators need go into the Helm chart too (see the setting-lifecycle skill and Configuration).

More: coding principles.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
Tool Version Notes JDK 21 CI builds with JDK 21. The runtime images run on Temurin 25 JRE. Gradle wrapper (./gradlew) Do not install Gradle yourself; the wrapper pins the version. Docker recent Needed for images, PostgreSQL tests and end-to-end tests (Testcontainers). kind, kubectl, Helm optional For the local quick start.

The build uses the EDC build plugin and a version catalog in gradle/libs.versions.toml, which also pins the upstream EDC version (edc = …).

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
Goal Command Build everything (compile, unit tests, Checkstyle) ./gradlew build Unit tests only ./gradlew test One module ./gradlew :edc-extensions:cx-policy:test Formatting check, as CI runs it ./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest checkstyleTestFixtures Javadoc ./gradlew javadoc Fat jar of a runtime ./gradlew :edc-controlplane:edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault:shadowJar Docker image of a runtime ./gradlew :edc-controlplane:edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault:dockerize OpenAPI specs ./gradlew resolve (output in resources/openapi/yaml/)

Integration-type tests are skipped by test unless you select them with -DincludeTags=…. See Testing.

docs.title: IDE
docs.text:
IntelliJ IDEA works out of the box: open the root build.gradle.kts as a project.

  • Import the code style resources/tx-codestyle.xml (Settings → Editor → Code Style → Import Scheme), or use the EditorConfig file resources/tx-codestyle.editorconfig.
  • Install the CheckStyle-IDEA plugin and point it at resources/tx-checkstyle-config.xml.
  • Every source file needs the license header. Templates are in resources/java.header and resources/hashtag.header.

Details: style guide.

docs.title: Run a connector locally
docs.text:
The quickest option is the in-memory runtime, which contains a control plane and a data plane in one process:

./gradlew :edc-controlplane:edc-runtime-memory:dockerize
helm install tx-inmem charts/tractusx-connector-memory \
  -f edc-tests/deployment/src/main/resources/helm/tractusx-connector-memory-test.yaml

The full setup with PostgreSQL and Vault on kind is described in the local quick start.

For debugging in the IDE, most developers run an end-to-end test: it starts real runtimes in the same JVM, so breakpoints in any extension work. See Testing.

docs.title: Upstream EDC sources
docs.text:
Much of the behaviour comes from upstream Eclipse EDC. Read it at the version this repository pins, not from main of the upstream repository. The edc-upstream-sources skill of the Connector Sensei downloads and searches the exact sources:

.claude/skills/edc-upstream-sources/scripts/edc-src.sh --help

docs.title: Test types and tags
docs.text:
Tests are JUnit 5 and are selected by tags. A plain ./gradlew test runs only unit tests; everything tagged IntegrationTest (directly or through one of the annotations below) is skipped unless you ask for it.

Annotation Tag What it is Needs Docker none – Unit test no @ComponentTest ComponentTest Several real components, no external systems no @ApiTest ApiTest HTTP controller tests with REST Assured no @PostgresqlIntegrationTest PostgresqlIntegrationTest SQL stores against PostgreSQL yes @EndToEndTest EndToEndTest Real connector runtimes talking to each other usually @CompatibilityTest CompatibilityTest Current code against the previous release's image yes

docs.title: Run what CI runs
docs.text:
CI job Command Formatting ./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest checkstyleTestFixtures Javadoc ./gradlew javadoc Unit tests ./gradlew test Component tests ./gradlew test -DincludeTags="ComponentTest" API tests ./gradlew test -DincludeTags="ApiTest" PostgreSQL tests ./gradlew test -DincludeTags="PostgresqlIntegrationTest" -PverboseTest=true One end-to-end suite ./gradlew -p edc-tests/e2e/<suite> test -DincludeTags="EndToEndTest" -PverboseTest=true Helm docs up to date helm-docs in Docker, then git diff must be empty

The definitive list is .github/workflows/verify.yaml.

docs.title: End-to-end tests
docs.text:
End-to-end tests start real runtimes in the test JVM: a provider and a consumer, each with control plane and data plane, and, where needed, PostgreSQL, Kafka, S3 or Azurite in Testcontainers. Because everything runs in one JVM, you can set breakpoints anywhere.

Run one class:

./gradlew -p edc-tests/e2e/transfer-tests test -DincludeTags="EndToEndTest" --tests "*TransferPullEndToEndTest*"
Suite Covers catalog-tests Catalog filtering by access policy, BPN and groups; DSP 0.8 vs 2025-1 policy-tests Policy validation and evaluation, policy monitor transfer-tests Pull and push, token refresh during transfers, data flow API, agreement retirement edr-api-tests /v3/edrs edc-dataplane-tokenrefresh-tests Data plane token refresh management-tests Management API validators, delegated authentication discovery-tests /v3/connectordiscovery dcp-tests DCP, STS, DIV, credential spoofing bpn-event-tests Business partner group events cloud-transfer-tests, end2end-transfer-cloud S3 and Azure Blob transfers kafka-transfer-tests Kafka pull dsp-tck-tests Dataspace Protocol TCK dcp-tck-tests Decentralized Claims Protocol TCK

Shared fixtures are in edc-tests/e2e-fixtures/src/testFixtures/java/org/eclipse/tractusx/edc/tests/: participants, runtime extensions, helpers for policies and catalogs, and base classes such as ConsumerPullBaseTest.

The e2e-test-author skill lists suites, scaffolds new tests and runs them like CI:

.claude/skills/e2e-test-author/scripts/e2e.sh run transfer-tests TransferPullEndToEndTest

docs.title: Compatibility tests
docs.text:
They check that the current code still talks to the previous release. First build the stable image, then run:

./gradlew :edc-tests:runtime:runtime-compatibility:stable:connector-stable:dockerize_stable
./gradlew test -DincludeTags="CompatibilityTest" -PverboseTest=true

docs.title: Deployment tests
docs.text: CI also installs both Helm charts in kind on the three newest Kubernetes versions, runs helm test, and upgrades from the latest release. You can run the same locally with the local quick start.

docs.title: Writing good tests
docs.text:
• Prefer unit tests; use component and end-to-end tests for behaviour that crosses modules.
  • Name tests after behaviour, for example evaluate_whenGroupMissing_shouldDeny.
  • Use the existing fixtures and helpers instead of new ones.
  • Pin new Testcontainers images in a Dockerfile under e2e-fixtures/src/testFixtures/resources/, so Dependabot can update them.

docs.title: Development Documentation
docs.text:
• Coding principles
  • Project Structure
  • Repository Structure
  • Decision Records

docs.title: Fail-fast and Explicit Configuration
docs.text:
1. Configuration should be loaded and validated at extension initialization so that issues are reported immediately. Do not lazy-load configuration unless it is required to do so.
  2. Settings can be pulled from the extension context and placed into configuration objects, which are passed to services via their constructor.
  3. Service configuration requirements should always be explicit; as a general rule, do not pass a single configuration object with many values to multiple services.
  4. Annotate configuration keys with @Setting so that they may be tracked.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
1. Do not throw checked exceptions; always use unchecked exceptions. If an unchecked exception type needs to be defined, inherit from org.eclipse.edc.spi.EdcException.
  2. Do not throw exceptions to signal a validation error; report the error (preferably collated) and return an error response.
  3. Throw an unchecked exception if something unexpected happens (e.g. a backing store connection is down after a number of retries). Note that validation errors are expected.
  4. Only throw an exception when there is no remediation possible, i.e. the exception is fatal. Do not throw an exception if an operation can be retried.
  5. Generally, services should return a org.eclipse.edc.spi.result.Result (or a suitable subclass).

docs.title: Simplicity
docs.text:
1. Avoid layers of indirection when they are not needed (e.g. "pass-through methods").
  2. Avoid needlessly wrapping objects, especially primitive datatypes.

docs.title: General Coding Style
docs.text:
1. Use var instead of explicit types (helps with clarity)
  2. Avoid final in method args and local variables
  3. Use final in field declarations
  4. Avoid static fields except in constants or when absolutely necessary (you should be able to provide a reason).
  5. Use interfaces to define shared constants
  6. Use "minimally required types" (or "smallest possible API"), e.g. use ObjectMapper instead of TypeManager, or use a String instead of a more complex object containing the String, etc.
  7. Use either public members, which are documented and tested, or private members.
  8. Avoid package-private members, especially if only needed for testing
  9. Avoid protected members unless they're intended to be overridden.
  10. Use package-private classes if they're not needed outside the package, e.g. implementation classes
  11. Avoid using enums for anything other than named integer enumerations.
  12. Avoid using static classes as much as possible. Exceptions to this are helper functions and test utils, etc. as well as static inner classes.
  13. Use only camel case and no prefixes for naming.
  14. Avoid unnecessary this. except when it is necessary e.g. when there is a name overlap
  15. Use static imports, as long as code readability and comprehension is not impacted. For example,
    • use assertThat(...) instead of Assertions.assertThat(...)
    • use format("...",arg1) instead of String.format(...), but
    • avoid of(item1, item2).map(it -> it.someOperation)... instead of Stream.of(item1, item2). Also, avoid static imports if two static methods with the same name would be imported from different classes
  16. Avoid Optional as method return type or method argument, except when designing a fluent API. Use null in signatures.
  17. Avoid cryptic variable names, especially in long methods. Instead, try to write them out, at least to a reasonable extent.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
1. All handlers and services should have dedicated unit tests with mocks used for dependencies.
  2. Prefer unit tests over all other test types: unit > integration/component > e2e
  3. When appropriate, prefer composing services via the constructor so that dependencies can be mocked as opposed to instantiating dependencies directly.
  4. Use classes with static test functions to provide common helper methods, e.g. to instantiate an object.
  5. Use [METHOD]_when[CONDITION]_should[EXPECTATION] as naming template for test methods, e.g. verifyInput_whenNull_shouldThrowNpe() as opposed to testInputNull()

docs.title: Data Objects
docs.text:
1. Use the Builder pattern when:
    • there are any number of optional constructor args
    • there are more than 3 constructor args
    • inheriting from an object that fulfills any of the above. In this case use derived builders as well.
  2. Although serializability is not the reason we use the builder pattern, it is a strong indication that a builder should be used.
  3. Builders should be named just Builder and be static nested classes.
  4. Create a public static Builder newInstance(){...} method to instantiate the builder
  5. Builders have non-public constructors
  6. Use single-field builders: a Builder instantiates the object it builds in its constructor, and sets the properties in its builder methods. The build() method then only performs verification (optional) and returns the instance.
  7. Use private constructors for the objects that the builder builds.
  8. If there is a builder for an object, use it to deserialize an object, i.e. put Jackson annotations such as JsonCreator and @JsonBuilder on builders.
  9. Note that the motivation behind use of builders is not for immutability (although that may be good in certain circumstances). Rather, it is to make code less error-prone and simpler given the lack of named arguments and optional parameters in Java.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
1. Only store secrets in the Vault and do not hold them in objects that may be persisted to other stores.
  2. Do not log secrets or sensitive information.

docs.title: Extensions and Libraries
docs.text:
1. Extension modules contribute a feature to the runtime such as a service.
  2. SPI modules define extensibility points in the runtime. There is a core SPI module that defines extensibility for essential runtime features. There are other SPI modules that define extensibility points for optional features such as IDS.
  3. Libraries are utility modules that provide classes which may be used by other modules. They do not directly contribute features to the runtime.
  4. An SPI module may only reference other SPI modules and library modules.
  5. An Extension module may only reference other SPI modules and library modules.
  6. A library module may only reference other library modules.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
1. There should only be a root gradle.properties that contains build variables. Do not create separate gradle.properties files in a module.
  2. For external dependencies, do not reference the version directly. Instead, use the version catalog feature.

docs.title: Handling Null Return Values
docs.text: 1. In certain situations, null may need to be returned from a method, passed as a parameter, or set on a field. Only use Optional if a method is part of a fluent API. Since the runtime will rarely require this, the project standard is to use the org.jetbrains.annotations.Nullable and org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull annotations.

docs.title: Objects Serialization/Deserialization
docs.text: 1. TypeManager is the component responsible for json ser/des, you can also use the ObjectMapper inside it, but there should be no other ObjectMapper instance.

docs.title: Class Naming
docs.text:
1. A single implementor of an interface should be named <interface name>Impl.
  2. An implementor who is meant to be the default implementation for an interface but other are/can be defined used instead.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Services can implement one the following interfaces: ReadinessProvider, LivenessProvider, StartupStatusProvider and register with the HealthCheckService, thus reporting the service's readiness status through the observability API.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text: 1. Always close explicitly Stream objects that are returned by a service/store, since they could carry a connection, which otherwise would leak.

docs.title: Issue Tracking
docs.text: Issues are maintained in GitHub Issues.

docs.title: Reporting Vulnerabilities
docs.text: Vulnerabilities in the Eclipse Tractus-X code base are best reported directly to the Eclipse Foundation.

docs.title: Git Flow
docs.text: The Tractus-X EDC repository uses a Git Flow, with main as the development branch and releases as the release branch. Other branches should follow the naming conventions of feature/x or hotfix/x, though this is not strictly enforced.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: We use Java 17 with Gradle for dependencies and builds. We use Checkstyle for code formatting. Releases are in the form of Docker containers and Helm charts.

docs.title: 1. Setup Eclipse Dash License Tool locally
docs.text: For instructions on how to download the Eclipse Dash Tool executable, refer to the project's GitHub page.

docs.title: 2. Generate DEPENDENCIES file
docs.text:
The following call generates the dependencies file. This list is populated by deriving dependencies using the build tool (i.e., gradle), analysing them using an IP tool (i.e., Eclipse Dash Tool), and decorating the resulting report with additional information using a custom script.

Execute the gradle task allDependencies for creating an integrated dependency report over all sub-modules of the project (including isolated modules). To process the dependencies of a specific module (e.g., an individual launcher) execute the standard dependencies task.

First, the dependencies of this module are calculated with gradle and passed to the Dash tool:

gradle allDependencies | grep -Poh "(?<=\s)[\w.-]+:[\w.-]+:[^:\s]+" | sort | uniq | java -jar /path/org.eclipse.dash.licenses-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar - -summary DEPENDENCIES

Note: on some machines (e.g. macOS) the ack tool should be used instead of grep.

docs.title: 3. Resolve restricted Dependencies
docs.text:
If a dependency is restricted, it is not approved by the Eclipse Foundation, yet. The Eclipse Bot is able to approve dependencies automatically, if the license can be resolved by ClearlyDefined.

  1. (optional) Visit https://clearlydefined.io/harvest and harvest the dependency from maven central.
  2. Create the Eclipse IP Issues or ask an Eclipse Commiter to do this for you.

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text: The repository for Tractus-X EDC contains the following:

docs.title: Tractus-X EDC Connector distributions
docs.text:
The repository provides distributions of the EDC Connector. The configurations for these can be found under the folders edc-controlplane and edc-dataplane.

  • edc-runtime-memory: Bundles a control and dataplane in a single runtime with in-memory persistence. This distribution is mostly suitable for local development and testing.
  • edc-controlplane-base and edc-dataplane-base: This configuration bundles all core components of the EDC Connector control plane as well as specific tractus-x EDC extensions. They are used as base for other distributions.
  • edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault: Starts with the controlplane-base but adds PostgreSQL as persistence and HashiCorp Vault as secrets backend.
  • edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault: Similar to the control plane distribution but for an EDC Connector data plane.

These distributions are packaged and published to maven central and to docker hub.

docs.title: EDC Connector Extensions
docs.text: The core EDC Connector is extensible by design. Tractus-X EDC provides a myriad of extensions that serve specific use cases. These extensions and their documentation are available under the edc-extensions folder and each should provide its own documentation.

docs.title: Helm Charts for EDC Deployment
docs.text: To facilitate deployment of these different builds and their prerequisites, Helm charts are provided. The charts and their documentation can be found here.

docs.title: End-to-End Tests
docs.text: A test suite composed of a set of end-to-end tests is provided under the edc-tests folder. They test the functionality of the EDC Connector in a black-box manner and should cover most of the tractus-x use case requirements. The tests instantiate runtimes built using the base control and dataplane distributions.

docs.title: Core and spi
docs.text: Contains core tractusx-edc modules and interfaces that are used by tractusx-edc extensions.

docs.title: Samples
docs.text: Might contain sample code that demonstrates how to use certain extensions or functionalities of tractusx-edc.

docs.title: Overview: Endpoint Topologies
docs.text:
Bidirectional data transfers involve transmissions that can be sent by either the provider or consumer during the transfer's lifetime. The provider sends data over a forward channel, while the client uses a response channel to send data related to the forward transmission. For example, a provider sends parts data over the forward channel, while the consumer sends data related to errors in the forward transmission via the response channel.

Bidirectional data transfers should be modeled using a single Dataspace Protocol offer and contract agreement. In other words, a single offer represents the ability to send both forward and response messages, while an active contract agreement can be used to initiate the transfer.

Bidirectional flows can be implemented using a variety of wire protocols, for example, HTTP or a messaging layer. However, all scenarios correspond to one of two endpoint topologies:

  • The consumer offers the forward channel endpoint, and the provider offers the response channel endpoint.
  • The provider offers both the forward and response channel endpoints.

The Dataspace Protocol (DSP) defines two categories of data transfer: push and pull. The endpoint topologies correlate to these categories as follows:

Provider Push Consumer Pull Consumer offers the forward channel endpoint; provider offers the response channel endpoint Provider offers the forward and response channel endpoints

In each case, the provider always offers the response channel.

docs.title: The Data Plane
docs.text:
The Data Plane establishes data transfer communication channels and endpoints using a wire protocol. There are many ways to do this, two of which are described below.

HTTP Endpoints

The forward and response channels are separate endpoints. The endpoints may be static, where all messages in a particular direction are sent to the same endpoint, which then uses a correlation mechanism to process them, for example, https://test.com/forwardChannel and https//test.com/responseChannel. Or, the endpoints may be dynamic, where a path part contains a correlation ID, for example, https://test.com/transferId/forwardChannel and https://test.com/transferId/responseChannel.

Queues and Pub/Sub

In this scenario, the forward channel is a queue or a pub/sub topic while the response channel is a queue. This is a typical architecture used when designing systems with Message-Oriented-Middleware.

docs.title: Required Changes to the Data Plane Framework
docs.text: The required changes to the Data Plane Framework to support bidirectional data transfers are minimal.

docs.title: Response Endpoint DataAddress
docs.text: The DataAddress in the DataFlowResponseMessage must contain a https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/responseChannel property of type DataAddress. This DataAddress follows the same format as the outer DataAddress and represents the response channel endpoint. For example, it may contain authorization data the consumer uses to access the response channel endpoint.

docs.title: The DataPlaneManager
docs.text:
The DataPlaneManagerImpl and its collaborators will need to be refactored to generate response channel DataAddresses:

  • DataPlaneManagerImpl must be modified to return an EDR in the case of a provider PUSH. This EDR will only contain a https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/responseChannel entry. The manager will delegate to DataPlaneAuthorizationService to generate the response.
  • DataPlaneAuthorizationServiceImpl must be enhanced to support responseChannel generation. This should be keyed off of the transfer type. As part of this process, a DataPlaneAuthorizationServiceImpl.createEndpointDataReference must generate a responseChannel endpoint by delegating to a new method PublicEndpointGeneratorService.generateCallbackFor(sourceDataAddress). Access Tokens can be generated from DataPlaneAccessTokenService.

docs.title: Technical Considerations
docs.text:
The above changes can work with both DSP pull and push scenarios. However, it is important to note a potential race condition that could be introduced in PUSH transfers. Namely, provider-pushed data could potentially arrive before the DSP start message containing the response channel DataAddress is received by the client. This is due to the nature of asynchronous communications. In this case, the client would either need to skip sending a response or store the response messages to send when it receives the response channel DataAddress.

The response channel lifetime is tied to the forward channel. For example, when the forward channel is closed, the response channel will also be closed.

docs.title: Catena-X Standardization and Tractus-X Support
docs.text: To achieve interoperability, Catena-X would need to standardize a bidirectional transfer type similar to its support of HTTP push/pull and S3 types. This could then be implemented in Tractus-X EDC.

docs.title: Connector Sensei
docs.text:
The Connector Sensei is an AI agent for developing and operating Tractus-X EDC. It knows this repository, the upstream Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC) version it is built on, and the specifications behind both: DSP, DCP, ODRL/JSON-LD and the Catena-X standards. It answers from evidence it opens in the session, such as source code, configuration, docs and specs, and cites file:line. It does not answer from memory.

It works with Claude Code and GitHub Copilot. Its procedures and deterministic helper scripts, the skills, are shared by both. How the skills work explains the idea behind them.

  • Skills
