  • Using the scripts without an AI
  • What the Sensei does and does not do
  • Maintaining the Sensei
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
The Sensei has 10 skills. It loads the one whose description matches your request, runs its script and follows its procedure; you can run the scripts yourself too.

  • EDC upstream sources

    Read, search and diff upstream Eclipse EDC (org.eclipse.edc) source code and SQL schemas at the exact version Tractus-X EDC depends on, or any other version.

    edc-src.sh

    edc-upstream-sources

  • Upstream EDC bump

    Upgrade Tractus-X EDC to a new upstream Eclipse EDC version (the edc entry in gradle/libs.versions.toml).

    bump-impact.sh

    upstream-edc-bump

  • Setting lifecycle

    Add, rename, deprecate, remove or look up a Tractus-X EDC configuration setting end to end, covering the @Setting declaration, env var, Helm template, values.yaml, helm-docs README, extension README, migration guide and tests.

    setting-trace.sh

    setting-lifecycle

  • Breaking-change guard

    Review a Tractus-X EDC change set (branch, PR or working tree) for changes that break operators, adopters or other dataspace participants, and for missing follow-ups.

    bc-scan.sh

    breaking-change-guard

  • New extension

    Create a new Tractus-X EDC extension or SPI module the way this repository does it.

    scaffold-extension.sh

    new-extension

  • SQL migration

    Create, review or debug Tractus-X EDC PostgreSQL Flyway migrations (edc-extensions/migrations).

    migrations.sh

    sql-migration

  • E2E test author

    Write, run and debug Tractus-X EDC end-to-end tests (edc-tests/e2e/*) that start real consumer and provider connector runtimes, with Postgres, DCP, Kafka or cloud storage via Testcontainers.

    e2e.sh

    e2e-test-author

  • Management API endpoint

    Add, change, version or deprecate a Tractus-X EDC HTTP endpoint (Management API extensions such as /v3/edrs, /v3/business-partner-groups, /v3/connectordiscovery, /v3/dataflows, or data plane public, proxy and token APIs).

    api-inventory.sh

    management-api-endpoint

  • Migration guide and ADR

    Write Tractus-X EDC migration guides (docs/migration/.md) and architecture decision records (docs/development/decision-records//README.md) in the repository's exact format, drafted from evidence (breaking-change scan, upstream version change, new DB migrations, commits since the last release).

    draft-migration-guide.sh new-adr.sh

    migration-guide-and-adr

  • Dependencies and Eclipse Dash

    Check third-party dependency licenses for Tractus-X EDC with Eclipse Dash before merging.

    dash-check.sh

    dependencies-and-dash

Each card opens the skill's procedure. Skills lists them in one table.

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text: Path Purpose .claude/agents/connector-sensei.md The agent for Claude Code (subagent definition: persona, knowledge map, ground rules, playbooks) .github/agents/connector-sensei.agent.md The same agent for GitHub Copilot (custom agent), with the avatar as icon .github/copilot-instructions.md Repository-wide Copilot instructions: Copilot adopts the Sensei identity and its rules even when the agent is not selected .claude/skills/ The skills: one folder per task with SKILL.md (procedure) and scripts/ (deterministic tooling). Loaded by Claude Code and Copilot. .github/agents/REUSE.toml License information for the avatar images (CC-BY-4.0) .github/agents/connector-sensei-profile.jpg Close-up profile avatar (256px) used in the GitHub comment header comment-template.md The template the Sensei uses on GitHub (issues, comments, PR descriptions, reviews): avatar header, AI disclosure, evidence section, sign-off

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The agent itself needs only Claude Code or GitHub Copilot with this repository open. The skill scripts use standard tools:

Tool Needed for git, bash (3.2+ is enough, i.e. stock macOS), awk, sed, unzip, curl, perl All scripts JDK 17+ and the Gradle wrapper Builds and tests, dash-check.sh, scaffold-extension.sh verification Docker Running E2E and PostgresqlIntegrationTest suites (Testcontainers) Network access to Maven Central, repo.eclipse.org and eclipse-tractusx.github.io Downloading upstream sources the first time, Eclipse Dash, the published DEPENDENCIES

Upstream EDC sources are cached in ~/.cache/edc-sources, outside the repository. The first lookup for a version takes up to a minute; later ones are instant.

docs.title: Using it with Claude Code
docs.text:
1. Open a Claude Code session in the repository root (or a worktree of it). The agent and the skills are picked up from .claude/ automatically. Start a new session after pulling changes to them.
  2. Ask for the Sensei by name, or run /agents to see it:
Ask the connector-sensei: why does my contract negotiation end in TERMINATED with a BPN group policy?

Claude also delegates to the Sensei on its own when a request matches its description (Tractus-X EDC, EDC, DSP, DCP, policies, Helm/config, upgrades, debugging, extensions). 3. Skills are loaded when a task matches their description. You can also name one explicitly:

Use the breaking-change-guard skill on my branch and tell me what still needs a migration-guide entry.

docs.title: Start a chat from the command line
docs.text:
Install Claude Code once (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code) and run claude once to sign in. Then, from the repository root or a worktree of it:

# Chat with the Sensei: the whole session runs as the agent
claude --agent connector-sensei

# The same, with your first question already asked
claude --agent connector-sensei "Why does my contract negotiation end in TERMINATED with a BPN group policy?"

# One answer printed to the terminal, then exit (quick lookups, scripts)
claude --agent connector-sensei -p "Which setting configures the BDRS server URL?"

# Continue your last chat in this directory
claude --agent connector-sensei --continue

Plain claude works too: Claude then hands questions to the Sensei when they match its description (step 2 above). With --agent, the Sensei answers every message itself, with its persona and rules from the first line. To make it your default in this repository, put {"agent": "connector-sensei"} in .claude/settings.local.json (personal settings, keep them out of commits).

docs.title: Using it with GitHub Copilot
docs.text:
• VS Code (Copilot Chat, agent mode): open the repository, open the chat, and select Connector Sensei in the agent picker. Reload the window if it does not appear yet. Copilot loads the skills from .claude/skills/ in agent mode.
  • Copilot on github.com (coding agent): custom agents in .github/agents/ can be selected when you hand a task or issue to Copilot. The repository-wide .github/copilot-instructions.md also applies to Copilot code review and PR descriptions.
  • Without selecting the agent: because of .github/copilot-instructions.md, Copilot still speaks as the Sensei and follows its ground rules (verify before asserting, cite sources, run bc-scan.sh before writing a PR description).

docs.title: What to ask: example requests
docs.text:
Goal Example request Skill(s) the Sensei uses Understand a concept "Explain how the EDR refresh works between consumer and provider, with the classes involved." edc-upstream-sources Find a setting "What is the env var and Helm value for the BDRS URL, and where is it read?" setting-lifecycle Add or rename a setting "Rename tx.edc.foo.bar to tx.edc.foo.baz with a deprecation period." setting-lifecycle, breaking-change-guard Upgrade upstream EDC "Plan the upgrade from EDC 0.17.0 to 0.18.0: what breaks, which migrations do we need?" upstream-edc-bump, edc-upstream-sources, sql-migration Adopt an upstream change "Upstream deprecated EndpointDataReferenceEntry in 0.17.0. Where do we use it and how should we migrate?" edc-upstream-sources Review a PR "Review PR #1234 for breaking changes and missing follow-ups." breaking-change-guard Prepare a release "Draft the 0.13 → 0.14 migration guide." migration-guide-and-adr, setting-lifecycle Record a decision "Create a decision record for caching DID documents and fill the rationale from our discussion." migration-guide-and-adr New feature module "Where should a Factory-X-agnostic notification extension live? Scaffold it." new-extension Schema change "Add an index on edc_transfer_process.state and tell me what to test." sql-migration Prove a feature end to end "Write an E2E test that a BPN group policy hides the offer from other consumers." e2e-test-author New endpoint "Add GET /v3/edrs/{id}/status, following our API conventions." management-api-endpoint Write documentation "Add a page on configuring the Kafka extension to the documentation site, with the settings from the code." setting-lifecycle, edc-upstream-sources Review documentation "Check docs/deployment/helm-chart.md against the chart and list what is out of date." setting-lifecycle Dependency hygiene "Does bumping com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind introduce restricted licenses?" dependencies-and-dash

Good requests name the side (consumer or provider), the version (deployed release, DSP version) and paste evidence (log excerpt, request payload, error). The Sensei asks for them when they matter.

docs.title: Using the scripts without an AI
docs.text:
Every script is a plain shell script. Run them yourself, in CI, or in a pre-push hook. All print --help.

S=.claude/skills
$S/edc-upstream-sources/scripts/edc-src.sh read DcpIdentityService        # upstream class at the pinned version
$S/upstream-edc-bump/scripts/bump-impact.sh 0.17.0 0.18.0                  # impact report of an EDC bump
$S/setting-lifecycle/scripts/setting-trace.sh TX_EDC_IAM_DCP_BDRS_SERVER_URL
$S/breaking-change-guard/scripts/bc-scan.sh --strict                       # exit 1 on BLOCKER/BREAKING
$S/new-extension/scripts/scaffold-extension.sh edc-extensions/cx-foo org.eclipse.tractusx.edc.foo CxFooExtension
$S/sql-migration/scripts/migrations.sh status
$S/e2e-test-author/scripts/e2e.sh list
$S/management-api-endpoint/scripts/api-inventory.sh
$S/migration-guide-and-adr/scripts/draft-migration-guide.sh --branch HEAD
$S/dependencies-and-dash/scripts/dash-check.sh --list-only

The full catalog, including planned skills, is in .claude/skills/README.md.

docs.title: What the Sensei does and does not do
docs.text:
Does: - Opens the code, the upstream sources at the pinned version, specs and standards before it answers, and cites them. - Says whether behaviour comes from Tractus-X, upstream EDC, a specification or a Catena-X standard. - Runs the skill scripts to collect facts, then gives a recommendation with the concrete next step: a payload, config, command, patch or test. - Speaks in first person, in the voice of a calm dojo master, while code and config stay exact.

Does not: - Change files unless you ask it to implement something. By default it is an advisor. - Push, open PRs or post comments on its own. You stay in control of everything outward-facing. - Replace review. Its output is a proposal. AI-generated contributions carry the AI disclosure header (see the skill files) and must be reviewed and verified by the human contributor who submits them.

docs.title: Maintaining the Sensei
docs.text:
• Keep both agent files in sync. .claude/agents/connector-sensei.md and .github/agents/connector-sensei.agent.md share the same body; only the front matter differs.
  • Add a skill by following How the skills work → Writing a new skill. Then list it in .claude/skills/README.md, in the skill table of both agent files, and in .github/copilot-instructions.md.
  • License headers: AI-generated files carry the Apache-2.0 header with the AI disclosure block (AI-generated portions under CC0-1.0, SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 AND CC0-1.0, Assisted-By:). Images are covered by .github/agents/REUSE.toml.
  • Posting on GitHub as the Sensei: use comment-template.md. It keeps the avatar, the AI disclosure and the evidence section consistent across issues, PRs and reviews.
  • After an upstream EDC bump, re-run the skill scripts once against the new version. They read the version from gradle/libs.versions.toml, so they normally need no change.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix The Sensei or a skill does not show up Start a new Claude Code session, or reload the VS Code window, after pulling. Check that the files are on your branch. edc-src: no org.eclipse.edc artifacts in the Gradle cache Run ./gradlew compileJava once so Gradle resolves the upstream artifacts. First upstream lookup is slow Sources are downloaded once per version into ~/.cache/edc-sources. Set EDC_SRC_OFFLINE=1 to forbid downloads. e2e: suite '…' needs Docker Start Docker (Testcontainers). e2e.sh compile <suite> works without it. dash-check.sh cannot reach the internet Use --list-only for the dependency diff; the Dash run needs repo.eclipse.org and the Eclipse/ClearlyDefined APIs. An answer cites nothing Ask it to show the evidence. Its rules forbid unverified claims, and it should say "I could not find X" rather than guess.

docs.title: Connector Sensei comment template
docs.text:
When the Connector Sensei writes on GitHub (an issue, an issue comment, a PR description or a review comment), it uses this template. Readers can then see at a glance that an AI agent wrote the text, which human posted it, and which claims the Sensei verified and which it only infers.

  • Rules
  • Template
  • Per kind of post
  • Avatar URL
  • Example

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Header and sign-off are mandatory: the avatar, the name, the AI disclosure and the GitHub login of the person who posts it. GitHub shows that person as the author, so the header keeps the post honest.
  2. The body follows the repository's own template for that kind of post. The Sensei template wraps it and does not replace it (see Per kind of post).
  3. The voice belongs to the prose: one greeting line and at most two proverbs. Code, payloads, paths, commands and tables stay exact and plain.
  4. Evidence section for any non-trivial claim: the commands that reproduce every number and path, and a clear split between verified and inferred.
  5. Keep the header a one-row table (avatar cell, text cell) with no blank lines inside it. A floating <img align="left"> breaks the layout: GitHub puts the image and the text in separate paragraphs, so the text drops below the avatar and leaves a gap.
  6. Mention the posting person with @ in the header (@<github-login>), so the post links to the human who is accountable for it. Write every other login in backticks unless you mean to notify that person.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
Copy everything inside the block. Replace <github-login> (written <github-login> inside the HTML) with the login that posts, keeping the @ and the <…> placeholders, and delete sections that do not apply.

<table>
<tr>
<td width="96"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc/main/.github/agents/connector-sensei-profile.jpg" width="88" height="88" alt="Connector Sensei avatar"></td>
<td>
<b>Connector Sensei</b> 🥋<br>
AI agent for Tractus-X EDC · <a href="https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc/blob/main/docs/development/connector-sensei/README.md">what is this?</a><br>
<sub>Posted through @<github-login>'s account at their request. I answer from code and specs I opened, not from memory.</sub>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

<one in-character greeting line, e.g. "I have walked through your change, my student." or "Greetings, keepers of the dojo.">

<body: the repository template for this kind of post, see "Per kind of post">

<details>
<summary><b>How I produced this (and how you can reproduce it)</b></summary>

Run from the repository root on `<branch>` @ `<short-sha>`:

```bash
<the exact commands whose output backs the claims above>
```

still to be confirmed, and how>.

</details>

docs.title: Per kind of post
docs.text:
Kind of post Body to use inside the template Greeting example New issue: bug .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.md "I have followed this failure to its root." New issue: feature or plan .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/feature_request.md (WHAT / WHY / HOW / FURTHER NOTES) "Greetings, keepers of the dojo." Issue comment Free form: lead with the direct answer, then evidence, then the next step "I have read this issue and the code behind it." PR description .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, after running breaking-change-guard "I have prepared this change, my student." Review comment (inline) Header line and sign-off only: keep the avatar at width="20", use one sentence for the finding, then the evidence (path:line) "I have walked through your change, my student."

For short inline review comments, use the compact header instead of the full one:

docs.title: Avatar URL
docs.text:
GitHub does not resolve repository-relative paths in issues and comments, so the avatar must be an absolute URL. The avatar is .github/agents/connector-sensei-profile.jpg: a 256×256 close-up of the Sensei, cropped from connector-sensei-large.jpg, so it stays sharp at 88px on high-density screens. It is CC-BY-4.0, see REUSE.toml. The full scene connector-sensei.jpg (128×128) stays the Copilot agent icon.

  • Default: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc/main/.github/agents/connector-sensei-profile.jpg
  • Before the file is on main, or to make a post immune to later moves of the file, pin the URL to a commit that contains it: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc/<commit-sha>/.github/agents/connector-sensei-profile.jpg. Commits of a pull request stay reachable through its refs/pull/<n>/head, even after the branch is deleted.

docs.title: How the Connector Sensei skills work
docs.text:
The Sensei's skills split each development task into two parts:

  1. Deterministic scripts collect the facts. They answer "what is true in this repository and in upstream EDC right now?": which upstream types changed between two versions, where a setting lives, which migrations are released, which endpoints exist, which dependencies are restricted. The same input always produces the same output. They can be read, reviewed, run by anyone, and run in CI.
  2. The Sensei turns the facts into recommendations. It reads the script output together with the code, the specs and the project's decision records. Then it explains what the facts mean, recommends what to do, proposes concrete changes (code, config, migration, docs), and asks for the decisions only a human can make.

The human decides and reviews. Nothing is pushed or published without you.

  • Why split it this way
  • The flow
  • Anatomy of a skill
  • Design principles for the scripts
  • Worked examples
  • Catalog
  • Writing a new skill
  • Limits

docs.title: Why split it this way
docs.text:
Deterministic script Sensei (AI agent) Good at Exhaustive, repeatable fact-finding: diffs, inventories, cross-references, version comparisons Interpretation, prioritisation, explaining why, adapting a pattern to a new case, writing prose and code Weak at Judgement, context, "is this acceptable?" Remembering facts precisely: upstream EDC renames things often (IATP→DCP, DIM→DIV, v4alpha→v3, DSP 0.8→2025-1), and memory goes stale Output Reports with severities and path:line Recommendations, patches, documents, questions Trust model Inspect the script once, then trust its output Check its evidence, review its proposal

Scripts alone tell you that ContractAgreement changed upstream, but not what to do about it. An agent alone guesses from memory, and is often wrong about a fast-moving codebase. Together, the agent's reasoning starts from complete and current facts, and every recommendation can be traced back to them.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D([Developer]) -->|"request: e.g. 'plan the EDC 0.18 upgrade'"| S[Connector Sensei]
    S -->|loads matching skill| K[SKILL.md<br/>procedure + checklist]
    K -->|runs| X[[Deterministic script<br/>e.g. bump-impact.sh]]
    X -->|facts: report with<br/>severities and path:line| S
    S -->|reads code, upstream sources,<br/>specs, ADRs| E[(Evidence)]
    S -->|recommendation,<br/>proposed changes, questions| D
    D -->|reviews, decides, commits| P[Pull request]
    P -->|same scripts can run in CI<br/>e.g. bc-scan.sh --strict| C{{CI}}
  1. You describe the goal in your own words.
  2. The Sensei matches it to a skill from the skill's description and loads its SKILL.md.
  3. It runs the skill's script(s) and reads the report.
  4. It verifies and deepens the facts by opening the code the report points to, the upstream sources at the pinned version (edc-upstream-sources), the specs and the decision records.
  5. It answers with a recommendation and the concrete next step. When you ask, it implements the change, again following the skill's checklist.
  6. You review. The same deterministic checks can guard the PR in CI.

docs.title: Anatomy of a skill
docs.text:
.claude/skills/<skill-name>/
├── SKILL.md          # front matter (name, description) + procedure, conventions, checklist, pitfalls
└── scripts/
    └── <tool>.sh     # deterministic helper(s): read-only unless they explicitly scaffold new files
  • description (front matter) decides when the skill is used. It names the task and the trigger phrases ("upgrade EDC", "rename a setting", "is this breaking?").
  • The SKILL.md body is the procedure the Sensei follows: where the truth lives in this repo, the house conventions (naming, versioning, deprecation, docs format), a checklist, and how to debug typical failures.
  • The scripts are the deterministic part. The procedure says when to run them and how to read their output.

Claude Code and GitHub Copilot both load skills from .claude/skills/. One copy serves both tools.

docs.title: Design principles for the scripts
docs.text:
1. Evidence, version-pinned. Upstream facts come from the exact EDC version in gradle/libs.versions.toml, read from sources jars (Gradle cache or Maven Central). Local clones and memory are never the source.
  2. Read-only by default. Scripts never modify existing repository files. Scaffolding commands only create new files and print the remaining manual steps.
  3. Reproduce CI where CI exists. dash-check.sh builds the dependency list with the same Gradle tasks as .github/actions/generate-and-check-dependencies. e2e.sh run uses the CI test tags. bc-scan.sh checks what the helm-docs and Checkstyle jobs would reject.
  4. Honest heuristics. Where a script guesses (e.g. "this looks like a removed setting"), it says so and grades the finding (BLOCKER, BREAKING, HIGH, WARN). The Sensei is told to confirm each finding.
  5. Output for humans and agents. Plain text tables, one finding per line, path:line, severities, and links to the next step.
  6. Portable. bash 3.2+ (stock macOS) and Linux, standard tools only, no new build dependencies.
  7. Tested against real history. Each script was validated on past changes of this repository, for example:
  8. bump-impact.sh 0.16.0 0.17.0 finds the claims columns that became V1_9_0__Add_ClaimsColumn.sql, and the newly deprecated EndpointDataReferenceEntry.
  9. bc-scan.sh reproduces the breaking changes of the IATP→DCP rename (#2684) and the participant-id change (#2742).
  10. dash-check.sh reproduces CI's result: 464 coordinates, 456 approved, 8 restricted.

docs.title: Adopting upstream changes (EDC version bump)
docs.text:
"Plan the upgrade from EDC 0.17.0 to 0.18.0."

  1. Facts. bump-impact.sh 0.17.0 0.18.0 lists the upstream types Tractus-X imports that were removed, moved or changed (ranked by how many Tractus-X files use them), upstream settings removed or added, and SQL schema deltas.
  2. Recommendation. The Sensei reads the diffs (edc-src.sh diff <Type> 0.17.0 0.18.0) for the high-impact types and the release notes. It groups the work: compile fixes, behaviour changes in overridden areas (DSP 0.8 backports, DCP, policy), new Flyway migrations for each schema delta, settings for the migration guide.
  3. Proposal. On request it applies the bump, fixes compile errors type by type, creates migrations with migrations.sh new connector …, and drafts the migration-guide section.
  4. Guard. bc-scan.sh and the test suites confirm nothing else broke.

docs.title: Adopting an upstream method or deprecation
docs.text:
"Upstream deprecated EndpointDataReferenceEntry. What should we do?"

  1. Facts. edc-src.sh diff EndpointDataReferenceEntry 0.16.0 0.17.0 shows @Deprecated(since = "management-api:v3"). bump-impact.sh shows that 7 Tractus-X main-code files (14 including tests) import it.
  2. Recommendation. The Sensei looks up the replacement upstream (edc-src.sh grep), compares it with how Tractus-X uses the type (EDR API, EDR callback, token refresh), and proposes a migration path. That includes whether the Tractus-X /v3/edrs API contract changes for clients.
  3. Decision for you. Adopt now or in the next minor, and whether a deprecation period for clients is needed.

docs.title: Updating documentation for a release
docs.text:
"Draft the 0.13 → 0.14 migration guide."

  1. Facts. draft-migration-guide.sh --branch HEAD collects the breaking-change scan against 0.13.0, the upstream version change, new migrations, and user-facing commits since the release. On the current branch it surfaced the removed Helm value postgresql.persistence.storageClass.
  2. Recommendation. The Sensei turns each relevant item into a numbered section in the house style, fills old→new tables with setting-trace.sh, and lists what it dropped and why.
  3. Decision for you. Which items operators really need, and the wording.

docs.title: Reviewing a pull request
docs.text:
"Review PR #1234."

  1. Facts. bc-scan.sh <base> reports released migrations edited, removed settings, Helm values, env vars and API paths, protocol-surface changes, and missing follow-ups.
  2. Recommendation. The Sensei confirms each finding in the diff and adds what the scanner cannot see (JSON-LD shape changes, semantics, security). It proposes fixes, such as deprecating instead of removing, or adding a migration instead of editing one.
  3. Decision for you. Approve, request changes, or post comments (it drafts them; you post).

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
See .claude/skills/README.md for every implemented skill with its script, and for the planned skills (cx-policy-constraint, connector-log-triage, multi-dataspace-split), which are documented as designs only.

Skill Deterministic part (facts) Sensei's part (judgement) edc-upstream-sources Upstream class, schema or setting at an exact version; diffs between versions What the upstream behaviour means for Tractus-X upstream-edc-bump Removed, moved and changed types; settings and schema deltas Upgrade plan, fixes, backports, migrations setting-lifecycle Every place a setting lives (code, env, Helm, docs, guides, tests) Rename and deprecation strategy, chart and doc changes breaking-change-guard Graded findings for a change set Confirm, add what is missing, propose fixes new-extension A module scaffold that builds green Placement (generic vs cx-), design, wiring sql-migration Folder status, next version, new file DDL/DML, idempotency, rollout e2e-test-author Suite map, test scaffold, CI-equivalent run Scenario design, fixtures, de-flaking management-api-endpoint Endpoint inventory (context, tests, docs, deprecation) API design, versioning, validation, docs migration-guide-and-adr Evidence since the last release; ADR skeleton The guide and decision text dependencies-and-dash CI-equivalent dependency list, Dash result, diff vs published Alternatives, pinning, IP review path

docs.title: Writing a new skill
docs.text:
1. Pick a recurring task with a clear fact-finding part. Look at what PRs and reviews repeatedly need (git log, review comments).
  2. Write the script first.
  3. Deterministic and read-only, or explicit scaffolding.
  4. --help text in the header comment.
  5. set -euo pipefail, and avoid grep -q in pipelines (SIGPIPE under pipefail yields false negatives).
  6. bash 3.2 compatible.
  7. The license header with the AI disclosure block, if AI-assisted.
  8. Validate it on real history. Run it against past commits or releases where you know the right answer, and keep the results for the PR description.
  9. Write SKILL.md. A precise description with trigger phrases, then where the truth lives, the procedure, the house conventions, a checklist and the debugging tips. Keep it under about 200 lines and link, rather than copy, long docs.
  10. Register it. Add it to .claude/skills/README.md, the skill table in both agent files, and .github/copilot-instructions.md.
  11. Consider CI. If the script's output is a pass/fail gate, it can also run in a workflow (for example bc-scan.sh --strict on PRs). That is a separate decision for the maintainers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Scripts are heuristics where they say so. A clean bc-scan.sh does not prove a change is compatible; the Sensei's review and the compatibility and TCK tests do the rest.
  • Some checks need Docker (E2E, Postgres) or network access (upstream sources, Eclipse Dash).
  • The Sensei proposes. Contributors remain responsible for what they submit, including the AI disclosure and the review it attests to.

docs.title: Tractus-X EDC Extensions for DataPlane Signaling Token Refresh
docs.text: This document details the architecture and implementation of the token refresh mechanism that extends the DataPlane Signaling framework.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The provider DataPlane exposes a new public facing API called the "Refresh API". Its purpose is to accept a refresh token and an authentication token (see documentation here), perform validity checks and then respond with a new refresh token similar to this:

{
  "access_token": "BWjcyMzY3ZDhiNmJkNTY...",
  "refresh_token": "Srq2NjM5NzA2OWJjuE7c...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires": 3600
}

A complete sequence including TransferRequestMessage is shown here:

  • (1)Consumer send TransferRequestMessage
  • (2) Provider sends DataFlowStartMessage to its own DataPlane via the Signaling API
  • (3) Provider's DataPlane creates an EndPointDataReference ( see here for an example)
  • (4) Provider's ControlPlane receives EndpointDataReference (= EDR)
  • (5) Provider sends TransferStartMessage that contains the EndpointDataReference to the Consumer via DSP. Consumer stores EDR for subsequent use.
  • (6) Consumer makes data requests against the Provider's public API (= data transfer). Those requests must carry the token from the EDR in the authorization header.
  • (7) Provider authorizes the data request

TOKEN EXPIRES

  • (8) The TokenRefreshHandler module creates the authentication_token
  • (9) The TokenRefreshHandler module sends token refresh request to provider's public Refresh API
  • (10) Provider performs authentication checks, creates a new access_token and a new refresh_token, updates internal records and sends the response back.

docs.title: Consumer: execute the token refresh
docs.text: There are three possibilities for how the consumer performs the token refresh. Which one is suitable for a particular customer will largely depend on the participant's deployment setup. These are not mutually excluding, they are merely different approaches that are all supported by Tractus-X EDC.

docs.title: 1. Automatic refresh using the (consumer) DataPlane
docs.text:
This is suitable for deployments that elect to use a data plane on the consumer side, effectively acting as HTTP client. Data requests are made by the consumer's data plane. Upon receiving an HTTP error code indicating an authentication failure (HTTP 4xx), the consumer data plane refreshes the token using the TokenRefreshHandler and retries the request. This is called "lazy refresh".

  • (1): Consumer data plane receives HTTP 401 indicating an auth failure
  • (2): The TokenRefreshHandler module creates the authentication_token
  • (3): The TokenRefreshHandler module sends token refresh request to provider's public Refresh API.

Note that if the token-refresh call also fails with an HTTP 4xx error code, the token must be regarded as invalid and not authorized. An expired contract agreement or an unsatisfied policy could be reasons for that ( see decision record and documentation).

Alternatively, implementations of the TokenRefreshHandler could choose to proactively refresh the token if nearing expiry instead of "letting it fail" first. This is transparent to the client application.

docs.title: 2. Automatic refresh using the /edrs API
docs.text:
In this scenario it is the client application making the HTTP request against the provider's data plane. To do that, it first has to use the /edrs API to obtain the access token. The /edrs API inspects the token and performs a refresh if required, then returns back a (possibly refreshed) access token to the client application:

  • (1): client application obtains token from EDR API
  • (2): EDR API (or a related component) checks if the token requires renewal
  • (3): EDR API triggers TokenRefreshHandler to make the refresh request
  • (4): TokenRefreshHandler calls refresh endpoint of provider data plane
  • (3)/(5): (refreshed) token is returned to client application

docs.title: 3. Manual refresh by the client application
docs.text:
Like in the previous section, this scenario outlines a deployment without a consumer data plane. The difference is, that in this variant the access token is not automatically renewed by the EDR API. This is suitable for client applications that need to maintain control over the refresh process, e.g. due to some backoffice user permission system. For those deployments Tractus-X EDC offers an endpoint in the management API POST /v1/token/refresh that client applications can use to trigger the token renewal.

  • (1): the client application requests the access token using the EDR API
  • (2): the client application makes the data request against the provider's data plane
  • (3): that request is answered with a HTTP 4xx indicating an auth error
  • (4): client application triggers the token refresh via the control plane Management API
  • (5) The TokenRefreshHandler module creates the authentication_token ( see documentation)
  • (6) The TokenRefreshHandler module sends token refresh request to provider's public Refresh API. Note that the TokenRefreshHandler module is the same as before, only that it is contained in the ControlPlane

docs.title: 4. Token refresh is handled completely out-of-band
docs.text: Consumer's control plane and data plane are not involved. This is a very specific use case, and is only recommended if neither of the other scenarios are viable. Note that Tractus-X EDC will provide no support for this scenario.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
To improve stability, reproducibility and maintainability of releases, tractusx-edc will undergo the following changes:

  • use EDC SNAPSHOT builds during development
  • use release versions of EDC in releases. Release branches must not change upstream dependency versions, unless there is a clear and concise reason to do so.
  • slightly update branching model
  • if possible, bugs/defects should be fixed on main and be backported to the respective hotfix/ branch
  • only hotfixes for critical security bugs will be provided as defined by the committers for the currently released version. Nothing else.
  • feature development happens in developers' forks only to keep the Git reflog of the origin clean.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Having releases depend on snapshot versions of upstream projects, such as EDC, is inherently dangerous, particularly when that dependency has not yet reached a final state and breaking changes are to be expected. Most problems will stem from breaking changes, such as Java SPIs, APIs and changes in service contracts.

Up until now, the only way out was cherry-picking, which is extremely cumbersome and error-prone, and requires a parallel build pipeline to publish the cherry-picked artifacts of EDC (and potentially others). With the approach presented here, cherry-picking is still an option, but there are easier alternatives to it.

Every release version published by tractusx-edc must be reproducible at any time.

docs.title: Use EDC SNAPSHOT versions during development
docs.text: During feature development we only use -SNAPSHOT versions of EDC packages. It is assumed that when the build breaks due to changes in upstream, the fix can be done quickly and easily, much more so than working off technical debt that would otherwise accumulate over several months. Builds on main are therefore not repeatable, but that downside is easily offset by the tighter alignment with and smaller technical debt and integration pain with the upstream EDC.

docs.title: Use release versions of EDC in releases
docs.text:
First, a new branch release/X.Y.Z based off of main is created. This can either be done on HEAD, or - if desired - on a particular ref. The latter case is relevant if there are already features in main that are not scoped for a particular release.

Second, the dependency onto EDC is updated to the most recent build. For example, if a release is created on March 27th 2023, the most recent nightly would be 0.0.1-20230326.

Updating Gradle files or Maven POMs, creating branches and tags in Git should be automated through GitHub Actions as part of the release process. For reference:

  • Modifying and committing files: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/26842#discussioncomment-3253612
  • Creating branches: https://github.com/marketplace/actions/create-branch
  • Creating tags using GitHub's API: https://github.com/eclipse-edc/Connector/blob/b24a5cacbc9fcabdfd8020d779399b3e56856661/.github/workflows/release-edc.yml#L21 ( example)
  • Create GitHub Release: https://github.com/eclipse-edc/Connector/blob/b24a5cacbc9fcabdfd8020d779399b3e56856661/.github/workflows/release-edc.yml#L56 (example)

Once a release is created, the EDC upstream version must not change anymore, unless there is good reason to do so, for example, a defect, that needs to be fixed upstream. At that point a decision can also be made to employ a cherry-pick model, in case the upstream's development has progressed to the point of breaking changes.

docs.title: Changes to the branching model
docs.text:
Tractusx-edc's branching model is already very close to the GitFlow branching model which is good. The following changes need to be made:

  • feature development happens in forks only. Thus, feature/ branches don't exist in the origin. This is important when moving to OSS.
  • adhere to GitFlow branch naming conventions, i.e. no docu, tryout_something branches. Increases readability and clarity, improves tool support.

Other guidelines w.r.t. the review process, merging etc. will follow in a later DR.

docs.title: A word on Bugfixes/Hotfixes
docs.text:
Once a release is published, for example 0.3.1 it will receive no further development other than hotfixes. Similarly, hotfix branches are created based off of the release branch, here releases/0.3.1, thus, hotfix/0.3.1. From this, three scenarios emerge:

  1. The actual fix is done on main and can be cherry-picked into the hotfix/0.3.1 branch. No new commits are made directly in that branch.
  2. The actual fix is done on main and must be manually ported into the hotfix/0.3.1 branch. One or several new commits are made on hotfix/0.3.1. This is needed when cherry-picking is not available due to incompatibilities between main and the hotfix branch due to intermittent changes.
  3. The fix is only relevant for the 0.3.1 hotfix, it is not needed in main. This can happen, when the problem is not present on main, because it was already implicitly fixed, or otherwise doesn't exist.

This might produce many branches, and the first hotfix makes the release obsolete, but it will greatly help readability and make a release's history readily apparent.

docs.title: Nightly builds
docs.text:
Nightly builds are generated according to a fixed schedule. Upstream EDC will soon begin to publish nightly builds as actual releases (as opposed to: snapshots) to a separate OSSRH-operated repository (see this EDC decision record).

Unfortunately there is no way to automatically trigger the tractusx-edc build whenever a new EDC nightly is created. The most reliable method is to periodically query for the latest EDC nightly, e.g. leveraging GitHub's dependabot feature, or using the following curl command:

curl <OSSHR_RELEASES_REPO_URL>/org/eclipse/edc/connector-core/maven-metadata.xml | xmllint --xpath "//metadata/versioning/versions/version[last()]" -

That would return something like to 0.0.1-20230213. As soon as the version string (here: Feb 13th, 2023) matches the current date, we can start the nightly. If the EDC nightly doesn't appear within a set timeframe, we throw an error.

docs.title: Notes for becoming OpenSource
docs.text:
• All artifacts (docker images, helm charts, Maven artifacts) should be published to well-known and publicly accessible locations such as MavenCentral, DockerHub, etc. The GitHub Packages repository is only accessible to authenticated users.
  • When the project was migrated to be an Eclipse project, we'll have to adopt the Eclipse Foundation's publishing guidelines, which prescribes the use of Jenkins for publishing to MavenCentral and OSSRH.
  • Typically, GitHub Actions should perform all verification tasks, running tests, etc. and Jenkins' only purpose is to publish.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Henceforth, testing shall be done in accordance with the herein outlined rules and definitions. As the guiding principles we shall establish:

  • separation-of-concerns
  • fast test execution speed
  • debuggability
  • low resource footprint
  • leverage features provided by, and adopt standards set by the Eclipse Dataspace Project
  • easy setup on developer systems

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Past experiences with tractusx-edc's testing setup has shown that it is time- and resource-consuming, which also makes it unreliable at times. Furthermore, a finer-grained test classification such as the one outlined in this document is currently neither present nor documented.

docs.title: Definitions and distinction
docs.text:
This section is largely taken from the EDC's testing documentation with a few amendments.

  • unit tests: test one single class by mocking/stubbing all collaborating objects.

  • integration tests: test one particular aspect of a software, that may involve external systems. Example: testing a particular object store based on PostgreSQL. External systems are to be provided out-of-band, e.g. through a CI pipeline or a script that runs on a local machine. Starting external systems from code violates the separation of concerns and it may also cause problems on some systems, e.g. when docker is not on the PATH, or not available at all. Integration tests typically only involve parts of a connector. A component test is a special form of an integration test, where real collaborators, but no external systems are used.

  • system tests: rely on the entire system being present. This is specific for each variant, for example testing a request against a system's API and verifying that a particular entry was created in the database. System tests involve one connector and the external service.

  • end-to-end-tests: similar to system tests, but they involve several connectors plus external services such as databases, identity providers, objects stores, etc. This type of test is used to verify that certain business requirements are fulfilled by simulating real user scenarios from start to finish, hence they are sometimes dubbed "business tests". For example, one would send a data request to a connector's public API and expect the connector to behave in a certain way and expect a certain response back. To keep things simple, end-to-end tests can be conjoined with system tests.

  • deployment tests: tests deployment artifacts such a Docker images or a Helm charts. The purpose of such a test is to verify the correct configuration and composition of an artifact, its purpose is not to test application logic. However, we can use normal requests to verify the correct installation. Sometimes this is referred to as "Smoke test".

  • performance tests: measure whether a certain iteration of the software fulfills pre-established performance goals. These tests are highly specific and may have dependencies onto specific hardware and network parameters.

It is a well-established fact that unit tests should make up for the majority of tests, because they are easy and quick to write and quick to execute, whereas integration and end-to-end tests are usually more complex and time-consuming to write and run.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Generally we should aim at writing unit tests rather than integration tests, because they are simpler, more stable and typically run faster. Sometimes that's not (easily) possible, especially when an implementation relies on an external system that is not easily mocked or stubbed such as cloud-based databases.

Therefore, in many cases writing unit tests is more involved that writing an integration test, for example say we wanted to test our implementation of a PostgreSQL-backed queue. We would have to mock the behaviour of the PostgreSQL API, which - while certainly possible - can get complicated pretty quickly. Now we still might do that for simpler scenarios, but eventually we might want to write an integration test that uses a (containerized) PostgreSQL test instance.

docs.title: Adopt a "local-first" mindset
docs.text:
EDC provides a way to launch (multiple) embedded connector runtimes from within the JVM using the JUnit runner, see this module and the test runtime extension for reference. All tests except deployment tests should be implemented using this feature to offer an easily debuggable and maintainable test suite. We call this a "local first" mindset, because we primarily aim at running a test locally (possibly using manual setup of external services). Once we have that, we can execute the test in the same way on CI runners. It should not matter whether we run tests on developer machines or on CI runners.

As a general rule of thumb, we should aim at running as much code from the JVM as opposed to: in external runtimes such as Docker or Kubernetes.

docs.title: Running tests in CI
docs.text: External systems such as databases or identity providers should be setup "out-of-band" of the test, using a script or the CI pipeline's declarative syntax (e.g. GitHub Actions' services feature). If possible, we should employ external systems in a self-contained way, e.g. using docker containers, because that increases portability and decreases the potential for conflict, e.g. in always-on databases.

docs.title: DO
docs.text:
• use integration tests sparingly and only when unit tests are not practical
  • deploy the external system as service directly in the workflow or
  • use a dedicated always-on test instance if provisioning is complicated and time-consuming (e.g. CosmosDB)
  • adopt a local-first mindset, i.e. aim at running test code inside the JVM.
  • take into account that external systems might experience transient failures or have degraded performance, so test methods should have a timeout so as not to block the runner indefinitely.
  • use randomized strings for things like database/table/bucket/container names, etc., especially when the external system does not get destroyed after the test.
  • use the class annotations provided by EDC to categorize and configure test execution

docs.title: DO NOT
docs.text:
• try to cover everything with integration tests. It's typically a code smell if there are no corresponding unit tests for an integration test.
  • slip into a habit of testing the external system rather than your usage of it
  • store secrets directly in the code. Github will warn about that.
  • perform complex external system setup in @BeforeEach or @BeforeAll
  • write tests that are opaque, or can only run in certain enviroments
  • use Test Containers, as it violates the separation of concerns. If external systems are needed, it should be an integration test.

docs.title: Test execution strategies
docs.text:
This section explains at which point in time we should execute which test. This is intended to minimize the impact on overall test execution time on CI, while still maintaining sufficient coverage.

Test type When to run Remarks Unit test when running tests locally, without any parameters, on every commit on every branch Integration test on every commit on every branch System/End-To-End test on pull request branches except when marked as draft Deployment test before merging pull requests and on every commit on main Performance test Only on a specific schedule, e.g. once per day or week

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC will move to Gradle as its build system. This decision record outlines the reasoning behind the decision as well as the migration path.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The primary motivator for migrating to Gradle is the overarching goal, set by the board of Catena-X, of pursuing an open-source methodology in general, and to track the Eclipse Datasource Components project in particular. While in theory that could be achieved with any build tool, much of what is useful or even necessary to achieve that goal, such as publishing to OSSRH/Sonatype and - in further consequence - to MavenCentral, has already been implemented in the EDC project. This reduces the implementation and maintenance surface of tractusx-edc with regard to the build, documentation and testing, and hence increases the development velocity considerably.

It is therefore a foregone conclusion to rely on technology that has already proven itself in the opensource community, instead of re-implementing (and maintaining) the same functionality all over again.

In detail, the aforementioned features are:

  • automatic and structured documentation using the autodoc plugin
  • generating unified OpenAPI documentation
  • default module dependencies
  • default configuration (POM, Swagger, artifact signing, code style,...)
  • default plugins for project submodules
  • publishing to artifact repositories (OSSRH/Sonatype and Maven)
  • unified and core-maintained version catalogs and version resolution strategies to avoid version clashes and runtime errors

This also contributes to much smaller, easier readable and more succinct build files. Since the build itself is executable code, a high degree of customization, optimization and modularization is possible.

Furthermore, developers can expect a much improved experience due to Gradle features like caching, task avoidance and parallelization resulting in faster and more responsive builds.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• convert Maven POMs to build.gradle.kts files, including BOMs
  • generate docker images using this plugin
  • convert maven profiles -> JUnit tags (cf. EDC): run tests using JUnit @Tags and the includeBuild feature
  • adapt documentation (i.e. exchange the commands)

docs.title: Further consideration
docs.text: Planned improvements regarding the testing procedure will also greatly benefit from the EDC build tools such as JUnit tags and conditional evaluation of the tagged tests. Much of EDC's testing framework is based on Gradle and can be seamlessly integrated in tractusx-edc.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Lombok library will be removed from the code base.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Lombok uses byte-code modification to achieve its goal. That is dangerous for a number of reasons.

First and foremost, to achieve its goal, it relies on internal APIs of the JVM, which are not intended for public consumption, thus they can and will get removed, refactored or made otherwise unavailable. This has been discussed at length in the project's GitHub page. This is especially problematic for an OSS project such as Eclipse Tractus-X.

Second, many of the features that are currently used by Tractus-X EDC are experimental (e.g. @UtilityClass) and are known to break some Java standard features, such as static imports.

Third, the value that Lombok offers is questionable at best (e.g. various constructor annotations, @Builder, @Value), because modern IDEs have ample features to generate boilerplate code. Further, it makes the code arguably less readable and less debuggable, very non-resilient against refactoring (@ToString(of = <FIELDNAME>)) and more dangerous (@SneakyThrows) at runtime.

Fourth and finally bytecode modification could conceivably cause problems in use cases where audited/certified code is required. Since the code gets modified during compilation in a way not covered by any spec, technically the runtime code could be significantly different from the source code. Although this problem is admittedly theoretical at the moment, we should not build those obstructions into the code base.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• Remove the lombok library from the version catalog
  • replace all annotations with actual code
  • [optional] add an entry to our coding principles to forbid byte-code modification (lombok, aspectJ,...)

docs.title: Further consideration
docs.text: We can even expect a slightly faster build, because "delomboking" will become unnecessary.

docs.title: Renaming Git branches to comply with Eclipse Tractus-X standards
Decision
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC will rename its Git branching structure to comply with TractusX release guidelines, and to be able to leverage GitHub convenience features, while continuing to use the Gitflow branching model.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The Eclipse Tractus-X organization has established a release guideline which mandates that all projects' default branch be called main.

docs.title: Selecting default branches
docs.text:
In GitHub, the default branch has a couple of important features attached to it:

  • cloning or forking the repository will automatically check out the default branch
  • when creating pull requests the default branch is targeted by default
  • automatic issue linking and closing only works with the default branch

docs.title: The problem with GitFlow
docs.text:
The GitFlow branching model suggests that the day-to-day work be done on a branch called develop, while the main branch stores the version history and only receives (merge) commits after a version releases.

This would call for develop being the GitHub default branch, which is forbidden by the aforementioned release guideline.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
In order to comply with the Tractus-X release guideline, to make use of the GitHub features and also use GitFlow, we propose renaming a couple of branches. While GitFlow suggests branch names, it does not require it, and most tools allow for customizing them anyway. Thus, from an abstract perspective, the following changes are necessary:

  • main becomes our work/development branch. All pull requests target main.
  • develop gets deleted
  • a new branch releases is introduced, which tracks the release history and receives post-release merge commits.

Technically this will involve force-pushing, which is a potentially destructive operation. Therefor the following section outlines the exact sequence of steps. Note that "upstream" refers to eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-edc, while " fork" refers to catenax-ng/tx-tractusx-edc.

  • create a new branch upstream/releases
  • create a new branch fork/releases, set it to track upstream/releases
  • push the contents of fork/main -> upstream/releases
  • synchronize upstream/develop with fork/develop
  • force-push the contents of develop -> upstream/main (do not update the tracking branch!)
  • synchronize upstream/main -> fork/main
  • delete/archive upstream/develop and fork/develop

Note that most of this will likely need to be done manually, since GitHub does not allow for advanced Git operations like force-pushing. Write access to upstream is required!

docs.title: Further notes
docs.text: The new releases branch (note the plural) will serve the same purpose that main did up until now, which is to track all releases (via merge commits and tags) in chronological order. We will continue to have separate release/x.y.z branches for every release.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The Helm charts provided by Tractusx-EDC will be refactored to be more focused and opinionated. Specifically, there will be the following charts:

  1. tractusx-connector-memory: all backing stores are memory-based and thus ephemeral. The vault will also be memory-based. This chart is intended for testing/demo purposes only!
  2. tractusx-connector: this is the "production-ready" chart that uses PostgreSQL and Hashicorp-Vault
  3. tractusx-connector-azure-vault: this is a variant of tractusx-connector-azure-vault that uses Azure KeyVault (" AZKV") instead of Hashicorp as some stakeholders still use AZKV.

These charts and their default configuration will be fully tested.

In addition to that, the Docker images will undergo some refactoring as well.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The current "dynamically composed" helm chart has proven to be a source for issues, and it is difficult to isolate errors due to the great number of variations. Further, only one particular variant (i.e. postgres+hashicorp) is put to any semblance of testing (i.e. business tests).

The official recommendation of Tractus-X EDC is to use PostgreSQL and HashiCorp Vault, and alongside it, we will provide charts for easy testing and setting up demos as well as an Azure KeyVault variant for legacy use cases.

Note: using Azure KeyVault is not officially supported or recommended by Tractus-X EDC!

This will also reduce the number of Docker images that need to be published.

docs.title: Variant 1: tractusx-connector-memory
docs.text:
This chart is intended for blackbox-testing or for easily setting up demos etc. It is not recommended for anything else. It will have the following properties:

  • all backing stores (Asset Index, Policy Store etc.) are ephemeral in-memory stores
  • the vault implementation will either be based also on memory, or on the FsVault, which uses local storage to store secrets
  • an embedded data plane will be used
  • no scalability or replication is possible
  • DAPS will be used as identity provider, so there is an implicit dependency onto a DAPS instance
  • the edc-runtime-memory Docker image will be used. That image contains both control plane and data plane.

docs.title: Variant 2: tractusx-connector
docs.text:
This is the production-ready chart that is published by Tractus-X EDC, and it will actually consist of two charts. One is the tractusx-runtime sub-chart, that contains all configuration for data plane and control plane, and the other one is the top-level tractusx-connector chart, that pulls in other charts as dependencies that are needed for one TractusX connector application. This is sometimes referred to as "umbrella chart".

Note: this will not include sub-charts for DAPS or MinIO.

tractusx-connector
  |-> tractusx-runtime
  |-> postgres
  |-> hashicorp-vault

The tractusx-runtime chart has the following properties:

  • PostgreSQL is used as persistence backend
  • HashiCorp Vault is used as secret store
  • the data plane is a separate runtime, i.e. separate pod
  • DAPS is used as identity provider
  • the edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault and edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault Docker images will be used

docs.title: Variant 3: tractusx-connector-azure-vault
docs.text:
This variant is essentially identical to tractusx-connector except for dropping the HashiCorp Vault chart, and replacing the HashiCorp Vault configuration with Azure KeyVault configuration.

For this, the edc-controlplane-postgresql-azure-vault and edc-dataplane-azure-vault Docker images will be used.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
There are several steps to testing our Helm charts:

  1. waiting for all pods to come up: using an exemplary configuration, this relies on the health checks, i.e. liveness and readiness probe (i.e. the runtime`s observability endpoints) to ensure that (most of) the static configuration is correct, no values are missing etc.
  2. executing a set of HTTP requests against the management API and assert a successful HTTP status code. For that we use Helm chart tests

Note: we refer to this kind of testing as "deployment testing"

docs.title: Docker image refactoring
docs.text:
The following changes need to be made to our Docker images:

  • rename edc-controlplane-memory -> -edc-runtime-memory
  • in edc-runtime-memory use FsVault instead of AzureVault
  • edc-runtime-memory contains an embedded data plane
  • rename edc-controlplane-postgresql -> edc-controlplane-postgresql-azure-vault
  • delete edc-controlplane-memory-hashicorp-vault

thus effectively resulting in the following structure:

edc-controlplane
|-> edc-runtime-memory
|-> edc-controlplane-postgresql-hashicorp-vault
|-> edc-controlplane-postgresql-azure-vault

edc-dataplane
|-> edc-dataplane-hashicorp-vault
|-> edc-dataplane-azure-vaul

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: From now on, Tractus-X EDC will use only conventional commit messages. The specification can be found here

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Conventional commits create a structured, explicit and unambiguous commit history, that is easy to read and to interpret. Conventional commits are widely used in the world of open source development. On top of that, there is extensive tooling to support the creation, interpretation and enforcement of conventional commits.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
As a first step, we enforce conventional commits as part of our CI pipeline. Tractus-X EDC is using Squash-Rebase-merging, and the PR title is used as commit message. We will not dictate how people structure their commits during the development phase of their PR, but we will enforce, that PR titles (and thus: merge commit messages) are in the conventional commit format.

To do that, we can use a very simple regex check on the PR title:

- uses: deepakputhraya/action-pr-title@master
  with:
    regex: '^(build|chore|ci|docs|feat|fix|perf|refactor|revert|style|test)(\(\w+((,|\/|\\)?\s?\w+)+\))?!?: [\S ]{1,80}[^\.]$'
    allowed_prefixes: 'build,chore,ci,docs,feat,fix,perf,refactor,revert,style,test'
    prefix_case_sensitive: true

That way, we can catch malformed PR titles early, which would result in malformed merge commit messages. In addition, we can use any of the tools linked above to ensure commit messages, e.g. when merge commits are altered manually, etc.

docs.title: Future outlook
docs.text: Once we have a structured commit history done in the conventional commit format, we can auto-generate changelogs, link to (auto-generated) documentation, render visually appealing version information, etc. Essentially, we can use any number of tooling on top of cc's. One key aspect would be to get rid of the manual changelog, see this discussion.

docs.title: Activate Checkstyle to enforce code style
Decision
docs.text: From now on, Tractus-X EDC will use activate Checkstyle, i.e. change its reporting level from WARNING to ERROR.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
We already have a checkstyle task in our Gradle setup, and our PR Etiquette document references the styleguide and mandates its use.

Our CI pipeline already uses checkstyle, but only outputs warning at the moment.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• in resources/tx-checkstyle-config.xml, Line 22, change <property name="severity" value="warning"/> to <property name="severity" value="error"/>.
  • fix all checkstyle errors

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will use Java 17 as baseline version.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Java 11 active support will end in September 2023, and, following Java "new" release cycle, we should update the baseline version to the current LTS from time to time. EDC upstream is switching to Java 17.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Remove the custom javaVersion and let the edc-build plugin set that when upgrading to the newest version of EDC.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Tractus-X EDC will use the iron-verifiable-credentials library for all processing of VerifiableCredentials and VerifiablePresentations.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The Eclipse Dataspaces Components project uses iron's sister library, titanium-json-ld for processing JSON-LD, which achieves close to 100% of conformance with the JSON-LD specification.

It thus stands to reason that we use iron-verifiable-credentials, because it supports issuing/verifying VCs/VPs, has support for JSON-LD (internally it also uses titanium-json-ld) and otherwise has a very light dependency footprint. which means high runtime type compatibility can be expected and minimal mapping/compatibility layers are needed. Crypto suites are pluggable, so in addition to iron-ed25519-cryptosuite-2020, which is also provided, we will implement support for JsonWebKey2020 which was mandated by the Catena-X consortium.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: • add support for JsonWebKey2020 to Tractus-X EDC using iron-verifiable-credentials.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will not maintain a manually curated CHANGELOG.md file anymore. Instead, we will rely on an automatically generated one. GitHub Releases offers that feature.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Manually curating a CHANGELOG.md is an arduous process, that does not offer any real value, rather, it introduces mostly problems. Chief amongst those are the fact that typically the curation happens shortly before the release, which increases pressure, and introduces the possibility that something is forgotten. Also, digging up the correct issue/PR numbers is a tedious process.

Relying solely on GitHub Releases fixes all that, because it will generate a succinct changelog, complete with issue/PR number and contributor.

We would lose the possibility to formulate "humanly readable" change log entries, but that is easily offset by the fact that we use conventional commits.

Thus, the commit log should be easily digestible and understandable, assuming a frequent release cycle.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
First, we need to fix the release process. It seems that at the time of this writing, the release PR contains all commits, instead of just the delta between main and the last release.

This is because upon merging normal PRs, we typically do a "Squash-And-Merge". The same thing was done on release PRs, which caused the git histories of main and releases to diverge.

For this to work, it is imperative to create a "Merge commit" for release PRs as that will preserve commits!

This is also reflected in the automatically generated changelog, for example 0.5.0-rc5. Once that is fixed, we can delete the CHANGELOG.md file and this GH action to update it (line 44).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The BPN validation extension will be improved in the following aspects:

  1. Instead of hard-coding them on policies, BPNs are stored in a database (in-mem + Postgres)
  2. BPNs are grouped to enable stable policies
  3. More Operators are supported
  4. Database entries can be manipulated using a REST API

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Hard-coding BPNs on policies is quite inflexible and does not scale, because when a new business partner joins or leaves the network, all participants would have to update all their policies, which is a significant migration effort. Instead, a structure has to be defined where that situation can be handled in a less intrusive and involved way. This effectively will remove the need to update/migrate policies.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Every BPN is associated with one or more groups, for example BPN0000001 -> ["gold_member"]. It is important to note, that these groups are internal tags that every participant maintains on their own, they are not claims in VerifiableCredentials (the BPN would be a claim, however). A new policy constraint is introduced, that looks like this:

{
  "constraint": {
    "leftOperand": "https://w3id.org/tractusx/v0.0.1/ns/BusinessPartnerGroup",
    "operator": "isAnyOf",
    "rightOperand": [
      "gold_customer",
      "platin_partner"
    ]
  }
}

NB: the leftOperand must be an IRI as mandated by ODRL, thus it must either be prefixed with the namespace (as shown in the example), or using a vocabulary entry in the JSON-LD context, i.e. tx:BusinessPartnerGroup. Supported operators will be: eq, neq, in, isAllOf, isAnyOf, isNoneOf.

Manipulating the BPN -> group associations can be done through a REST API.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The Tractus-X EDC dataplane will support the following proprietary extensions:

  1. AWS S3
  2. Azure Blob Storage

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. In addition to transfer over HTTP we need to be able to transfer larger files (i.e. Buckets).
  2. The packaged artefact (docker image, helm chart) should not require additional compilation or packaging.
  3. Broad coverage of use-cases with different extensions.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Previously, there was only support for AWS S3 which could be seen as problematic and favouritism. As such, the available support was extended with Azure Blob Storage to offer alternatives and cover a wider range of use-cases. According to this decision, the following protocols will be supported in the future:

  1. HTTP
  2. AWS S3
  3. Azure Blob Storage

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
To properly incorporate Azure Blob Storage and enable interoperability, all required extensions, i.e. HTTP, AWS S3 and Azure Blob Storage, will be bundled into the data plane image. This dataplane is then configured based on which extensions the user wants to use. Configuring specific features is entirely optional, and omitting to do so will cause that feature to be inactive at runtime.

Going forward, the Tractus-X EDC team will limit its efforts to critical bug fixes in the respective upstream repositories. As these extensions are proprietary in nature, the Tractus-X EDC Team will add no additional features beyond basic support.

The Sftp Protocol is another contender for integrating a more accessible protocol. It is however a low priority feature at the moment and will be postponed for future iterations.

Note: Azure Blob Storage will be integrated with Tractus-X EDC version 0.6.0

An application process for possible additional integrations will follow at a later date.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
What is the process for including/supporting additional Cloud Vendors?

Who will maintain the vendor specific solutions in the long-term (after the consortia phase)?

docs.title: Improving the issue quality and using a stale-bot
Decision
docs.text:
We will improve GitHub issue quality leveraging the following approaches:

  • provide a better issue template
  • introduce a stalebot workflow, that automatically closes zombie issues and PRs
  • reject (or let get stale) issues that aren't actionable
  • create a "backlog" milestone where we can put placeholder issues

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
We have seen quite a number of issues that are not actionable, because they lack detailed requirements, a definition of done, a motivation why the issue is needed or simply a proper description.

Some of it may have been caused by the auto-migration from Confluence to GitHub, some of it may have been caused by a lack of planning discipline. Un-actionable issues are useless, they clutter our boards and needlessly increase workload, because people periodically need to look at them. If an issue cannot be described in sufficient detail, it should be labelled appropriately, e.g. with question or triage.

We understand that it is not always possible to provide all required information at the time of submitting an issue. For those cases we will create a backlog milestone, that doesn't have a due date and on which those incomplete/placeholder issues should be planned. The backlog must be sanitized manually.

So in order to foster proper OSS hygiene we should aim for properly formulated, actionable issues, and periodically clear out ones that are inactive or have become irrelevant.

docs.title: Issue Template
docs.text:
We propose the following issue templates:

---
name: Feature Request
about: Request a new feature
title: ''
labels: triage
assignees: ''

---

## WHAT

// describes the desired functionality, how the feature should behave. This should include clear requirements, and a
// "definition-of-done", i.e. what the result of the issue should be. This is important for concept, documentation or
// ideation issues

## WHY

// outlines the motivation, why the feature is desired, and maybe what the impact is if the feature is _not_
implemented.
// "Because we need it" is not a sufficient reason!

## HOW

// if possible, outlines a solution proposal

## FURTHER NOTES

// anything else you want to outline

The existing bug report template is quite usable already, it contains the needed information. Bug reports should also receive the triage label upon creation.

docs.title: Stale-bot
docs.text:
• issues, that have the triage label get staled after 4 weeks and closed after 2 more weeks
  • issues, that have an assignee get staled after 4 weeks and closed after 1 more week
  • issues, that neither have an assignee nor a triage label get staled after 2 weeks, and closed after 1 more week
  • bug reports are ignored by the stale bot
  • issues in the backlog are ignored by the stale bot
  • pull-requests get staled after 1 week, and closed after 1 more week

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Implement token refresh for the Tractus-X EDC Data Plane according to the Tractus-X Refresh Token Grant Profile. This enables provider data planes to implement refresh tokens in an interoperable way for client applications using the Tractus-X EDC Connector.

Note refresh token support will be done almost exclusively in Tractus-X EDC, except for a few minor updates to upstream EDC.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Data providers may use short-lived tokens for HTTP client pull data transfers to enhance security. Refresh tokens allow data access to be maintained using short-lived tokens without starting a new transfer process.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The upstream EDC DefaultDataPlaneAccessTokenServiceImpl will be replaced to create a refresh token pinned to the client's DID. This TX implementation will use the following upstream EDC enhancements:

  • An upstream EDC decorator that adds the client DID as an extension property to the signaling request.
  • Upgrade the AccessTokenData type to allow for extensible properties to enable the AccessTokenDataStore to persist the renewal token.

Tractus-X EDC will implement token refresh based on the Trasctus-X Refresh Token Grant Profile

docs.title: TX DataPlaneAccessTokenService
docs.text:
An implementation of the DataPlaneAccessTokenService will be provided that overrides the default DefaultDataPlaneAccessTokenServiceImpl implementation. The TX implementation will do the following:

  • Create an expiring access token and set the expiresIn attribute of the DataAddress.
  • Create a refresh token that is returned in the refreshToken property of the DataAddress.
  • Provide a configuration option to set the refreshEndpoint property of the DataAddress. If not set, the refreshEndpoint property will not be included.

It will be possible for distributions not to include the TX implementation of the DataPlaneAccessTokenService and substitute another or revert to the EDC default implementation.

The refresh token will be sender-constrained to the client DID passed as part of the DataFlowStartMessage.

docs.title: OAuth 2 Refresh API
docs.text: The provider data plane will be extended to add a public API that implements the OAuth2 refresh_token grant. The refresh token will be verified according to the steps laid out in the Tractus-X Refresh Token Grant Profile. When a refresh request is successfully made, a new access token and refresh token will be generated and returned to the client. If a refresh token request fails due to a validation error, the associated access token and refresh token will be invalidated.

docs.title: Client-side Token Refresh
docs.text:
A client will be able to initiate a token refresh request in three ways:

  • Request data through a client data plane instance, which will check the token expiration and issue a refresh request if required. This behavior will be transparent to the client.
  • Request data directly and check if the access token is expired. If the token is expired, the client can call a client data plane management API to renew the access token.
  • Request data directly and handle access token renewal using OAuth 2 directly.

To support refresh token renewal, a DIM specific extension will be added that requests the authentication JWT to be signed using a key managed by DIM. This extension can use the same DIM API as the IATP extension.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Starting with the next release of Tractus-X EDC, the SFTP modules will be removed from the code base. Specifically transferprocess-sftp-client, transferprocess-sftp-common and transferprocess-sftp-provisioner.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: These modules don't implement any official Catena-X Standard, and as such, have not been part of any official Tractus-X EDC distribution for a significant period of time. Further, those modules are not up to the coding standards established by Tractus-X EDC, and would have to be refactored significantly. Even then, having dead code in a repository is bad hygiene, as it generates maintenance churn. Tractus-X EDC is not responsible for maintaining niche extensions, that are not officially sanctioned.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Starting with version 0.8.x of Tractus-X EDC, these modules will be deleted from the code base. At that time, stakeholders interested in continuing to maintain them are welcome to adopt them into their own repositories.

docs.title: Adopt a more regular release train of Tractus-X EDC
Decision
docs.text: Starting with 0.8.x, Tractus-X EDC will adopt a periodic release schedule of 6-8 weeks between versions. This increases the minor version, e.g. 0.8.0 -> 0.9.0 and breaking changes between those versions are to be expected.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
In an effort to minimize, technical debt, huge change surfaces and the probability of highly intense crunch times before a (Tractus-X) release, Tractus-X EDC will release roughly every two months. Note that this is completely independent from Tractus-X releases or Catena-X releases.

We also do this to give early adopters a chance to update their code base to new features and to shorten the feedback loop, as well as reducing the impact on continuous integration and testing, making the overall developer experience more agile and more manageable.

The EDC project has used this process for a long time with great success.

The commitment of the Tractus-X EDC team to maintain (= bugfix) the last version used in a Tractus-X/Catena-X release remains unchanged.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Weekly committer meetings serve as forum to do issue triage and priorization. We create GitHub milestones as a means of making our release schedule transparent and we plan issues for those milestones. The exact release date is determined by the committers and will be publicized in appropriate channels, e.g. Matrix.

docs.title: Improvements to the Tractus-X EDC versioning scheme
Decision
docs.text:
